database_name: F1 Verified Facts Project Memory Database

confidence_ladder.definition: Checked directly against an official FIA or Formula 1 source during database construction. Safe to state as fact and to cite.
A well-established record, consistently published in official sources over many years. Safe to rely on; cite the official archive if publishing.

Harvested from Wikipedia's season results tables, which are transcribed from FIA classifications. Every row was cross-checked on load against independently held season data. Reliable for results; not official under this database's policy, so cite the FIA/F1 archive if publishing.
Correct in substance. An exact figure or date may have drifted or may move with the current season. Confirm before publication.
Placeholder, disputed, or known to be incomplete. Never state as fact.

verification_policy.missing_fact_policy: Mark UNVERIFIED / NOT FOUND IN OFFICIAL SOURCES; never invent.
verification_policy.promotion_rule: Never promote a fact to 'verified' without an official FIA or Formula 1 source.
forbidden_as_authority: Fan sites, Reddit, secondary media, unsourced databases

coverage: Complete for: the chassis register (every chassis that has raced), engines, per-season entry lists, season champions, race-by-race winners 1950-2026, pole position 1950-2024, fastest lap 1950-2024 bar 12 races, the circuit of every race 1950-2026, constructor lineage, engine formulae, regulation changes, safety milestones, points systems. Partial by design for: full driver register (every race winner, pole-sitter and fastest-lap setter, not all ~780 starters); full finishing order; qualifying, grid and lap-by-lap data (not held); chassis specifications, which exist only on the per-car articles and are thin for the modern era because teams do not publish them. The chassis a race was won in is known where the season's entry list names one chassis for the constructor and NULL where it names several. See the known_gaps table.

seasons.engine_formula: 1.5 L supercharged or 4.5 L naturally aspirated
seasons.notes: Inaugural World Championship. Indianapolis 500 counted towards the title (1950-60) though almost no F1 regulars entered. No Constructors' Championship yet. Best 4 of 7 results counted.

seasons.engine_formula: 1.5 L supercharged or 4.5 L naturally aspirated
seasons.notes: Fangio's first title. Alfa Romeo withdrew at season's end when the FIA declined to fund its programme; gross total 37, net 31 after dropped scores.

seasons.engine_formula: Formula 2: 2.0 L naturally aspirated (F1 entries permitted but non-scoring in practice)
seasons.notes: Run to Formula 2 regulations after Alfa's withdrawal left too few F1 cars. Ascari won every race he entered.

seasons.engine_formula: Formula 2: 2.0 L naturally aspirated (F1 entries permitted but non-scoring in practice)
seasons.notes: Second consecutive title; Ascari remains the only Italian double champion.

seasons.engine_formula: 2.5 L naturally aspirated
seasons.notes: Fangio started the year at Maserati and switched to the new Mercedes W196 from the French GP. Mercedes returned to Grand Prix racing after an 15-year absence.

seasons.engine_formula: 2.5 L naturally aspirated
seasons.notes: Season truncated after the Le Mans disaster; the French, German, Swiss and Spanish rounds were cancelled. Switzerland has never held a championship race since.

seasons.engine_formula: 2.5 L naturally aspirated
seasons.notes: Fangio drove the Lancia-Ferrari D50. Peter Collins handed his car to Fangio at Monza, surrendering his own title chance.

seasons.engine_formula: 2.5 L naturally aspirated
seasons.notes: Fangio's fifth and final title, aged 46 — a record that stood until 2003. His Nurburgring drive is widely held to be the greatest of the era.

seasons.engine_formula: 2.5 L naturally aspirated
seasons.notes: First Constructors' Championship, won by Vanwall. Hawthorn took the drivers' title with one win to Moss's four, partly because Moss testified in Hawthorn's defence at Porto. Britain's first champion.

seasons.engine_formula: 2.5 L naturally aspirated
seasons.notes: The rear-engined revolution: Cooper's mid-engined T51 broke the front-engined orthodoxy for good.

seasons.engine_formula: 2.5 L naturally aspirated
seasons.notes: Last year the Indianapolis 500 counted. Five straight wins for Brabham mid-season.

seasons.engine_formula: 1.5 L naturally aspirated
seasons.notes: Title decided at Monza where Wolfgang von Trips was killed along with 15 spectators. Phil Hill became the first American champion.

seasons.engine_formula: 1.5 L naturally aspirated
seasons.notes: BRM's only championship, and Graham Hill's first.

seasons.engine_formula: 1.5 L naturally aspirated
seasons.notes: Clark's seven wins from ten starts in the Lotus 25 monocoque — the first fully stressed-skin F1 chassis.

seasons.engine_formula: 1.5 L naturally aspirated
seasons.notes: John Surtees remains the only person to win world championships on both two wheels and four.

seasons.engine_formula: 1.5 L naturally aspirated
seasons.notes: Clark won the Indianapolis 500 and the F1 title in the same year, skipping Monaco to do so.

seasons.engine_formula: 3.0 L naturally aspirated / 1.5 L forced induction
seasons.notes: The 3.0 L formula begins — 'the return of power'. Brabham is still the only man to win the title in a car bearing his own name.

seasons.engine_formula: 3.0 L naturally aspirated / 1.5 L forced induction
seasons.notes: Denny Hulme beat his own team owner. The Cosworth DFV debuted at Zandvoort in the Lotus 49 and won first time out.

seasons.engine_formula: 3.0 L naturally aspirated / 1.5 L forced induction
seasons.notes: Jim Clark killed at Hockenheim in F2, April 1968. Graham Hill held Lotus together to take the title. Sponsorship liveries appeared (Gold Leaf Team Lotus) and wings arrived at Spa.

seasons.engine_formula: 3.0 L naturally aspirated / 1.5 L forced induction
seasons.notes: Matra's only title, run by Ken Tyrrell. High-mounted aerofoils banned mid-season after failures at Barcelona.

seasons.engine_formula: 3.0 L naturally aspirated / 1.5 L forced induction
seasons.notes: Jochen Rindt killed in practice at Monza and became the sport's only posthumous World Champion. Lotus 72 introduced side radiators and torsion-bar suspension.

seasons.engine_formula: 3.0 L naturally aspirated / 1.5 L forced induction
seasons.notes: Tyrrell's first championship as a constructor in its own right.

seasons.engine_formula: 3.0 L naturally aspirated / 1.5 L forced induction
seasons.notes: At 25, Emerson Fittipaldi became the youngest champion to that point — a record held for 33 years.

seasons.engine_formula: 3.0 L naturally aspirated / 1.5 L forced induction
seasons.notes: Stewart's third title; he retired immediately after the death of team-mate Francois Cevert at Watkins Glen, skipping what would have been his 100th GP.

seasons.engine_formula: 3.0 L naturally aspirated / 1.5 L forced induction
seasons.notes: McLaren's first championship double, four years after Bruce McLaren's death testing at Goodwood.

seasons.engine_formula: 3.0 L naturally aspirated / 1.5 L forced induction
seasons.notes: Ferrari's first title in eleven years, built on the transverse-gearbox 312T.

seasons.engine_formula: 3.0 L naturally aspirated / 1.5 L forced induction
seasons.notes: Decided by one point in the rain at Fuji after Lauda's near-fatal Nurburgring crash and his decision to withdraw from the finale. The Nordschleife never held a championship race again.

seasons.engine_formula: 3.0 L naturally aspirated / 1.5 L turbocharged
seasons.notes: Renault introduced the turbocharged RS01 at Silverstone — mocked as the 'yellow teapot', it changed the sport.

seasons.engine_formula: 3.0 L naturally aspirated / 1.5 L turbocharged
seasons.notes: Ground effect arrives: the Lotus 79 'wing car'. Ronnie Peterson died from injuries sustained at Monza.

seasons.engine_formula: 3.0 L naturally aspirated / 1.5 L turbocharged
seasons.notes: Ferrari's last drivers' title until 2000. Gilles Villeneuve held station behind Scheckter at Monza rather than take the fight to his team-mate.

seasons.engine_formula: 3.0 L naturally aspirated / 1.5 L turbocharged
seasons.notes: Williams's first championship, eleven years after Frank Williams's first entry.

seasons.engine_formula: 3.0 L naturally aspirated / 1.5 L turbocharged
seasons.notes: Sliding skirts banned; Brabham's hydropneumatic ride-height system exploited the letter of the rule. Concorde Agreement signed, ending the FISA-FOCA war.

seasons.engine_formula: 3.0 L naturally aspirated / 1.5 L turbocharged
seasons.notes: The sport's darkest modern season: Gilles Villeneuve killed at Zolder, Riccardo Paletti at Montreal, Didier Pironi career-ended at Hockenheim. Keke Rosberg took the title with a single win.

seasons.engine_formula: 3.0 L naturally aspirated / 1.5 L turbocharged
seasons.notes: First turbo-powered drivers' champion. Flat bottoms mandated, killing ground effect.

seasons.engine_formula: 3.0 L naturally aspirated / 1.5 L turbocharged
seasons.notes: The closest margin in history: half a point. McLaren MP4/2 with TAG-Porsche power won 12 of 16.

seasons.engine_formula: 3.0 L naturally aspirated / 1.5 L turbocharged
seasons.notes: France's first World Champion.

seasons.engine_formula: 3.0 L naturally aspirated / 1.5 L turbocharged
seasons.notes: Mansell's tyre exploded at Adelaide with the title in his hands; Prost became the first back-to-back champion since Brabham in 1960.

seasons.engine_formula: 3.5 L naturally aspirated or 1.5 L turbocharged (boost limited)
seasons.notes: Naturally aspirated cars readmitted alongside boost-limited turbos. Piquet's third title.

seasons.engine_formula: 3.5 L naturally aspirated or 1.5 L turbocharged (boost limited)
seasons.notes: McLaren MP4/4 won 15 of 16 races — the most dominant single season by win rate. Prost scored more gross points (105 to 94) but lost on dropped scores.

seasons.engine_formula: 3.5 L naturally aspirated
seasons.notes: Turbos banned. Title settled by the Suzuka chicane collision; Senna disqualified. Last year of dropped scores.

seasons.engine_formula: 3.5 L naturally aspirated
seasons.notes: Suzuka again — Senna drove into Prost at Turn 1, settling the title on lap 1.

seasons.engine_formula: 3.5 L naturally aspirated
seasons.notes: Senna's third and final title. Michael Schumacher debuted at Spa for Jordan.

seasons.engine_formula: 3.5 L naturally aspirated
seasons.notes: The Williams FW14B with active suspension, traction control and semi-automatic gearbox. Mansell's nine wins were a single-season record at the time.

seasons.engine_formula: 3.5 L naturally aspirated
seasons.notes: Prost's fourth title, then retirement. Driver aids banned for 1994.

seasons.engine_formula: 3.5 L naturally aspirated
seasons.notes: Ayrton Senna and Roland Ratzenberger killed at Imola over one weekend; Karl Wendlinger critically injured at Monaco. The GPDA reformed and the FIA's modern safety programme began. Title decided by collision at Adelaide.

seasons.engine_formula: 3.0 L naturally aspirated, max 10 cylinders (V10 from 2000 mandated)
seasons.notes: Engine capacity cut to 3.0 L. Benetton's only constructors' title.

seasons.engine_formula: 3.0 L naturally aspirated, max 10 cylinders (V10 from 2000 mandated)
seasons.notes: Damon Hill followed his father Graham — the only father-and-son World Champions until Keke and Nico Rosberg in 2016.

seasons.engine_formula: 3.0 L naturally aspirated, max 10 cylinders (V10 from 2000 mandated)
seasons.notes: Schumacher finished second on the road but was excluded from the final classification for driving into Villeneuve at Jerez. Bridgestone entered, ending Goodyear's monopoly.

seasons.engine_formula: 3.0 L naturally aspirated, max 10 cylinders (V10 from 2000 mandated)
seasons.notes: Narrow-track cars and grooved tyres introduced to cut cornering speed. McLaren MP4/13 with the Newey-designed 'brake steer' controversy.

seasons.engine_formula: 3.0 L naturally aspirated, max 10 cylinders (V10 from 2000 mandated)
seasons.notes: Ferrari's first constructors' title since 1983 while Schumacher sat out with a broken leg from Silverstone.

seasons.engine_formula: 3.0 L naturally aspirated, max 10 cylinders (V10 from 2000 mandated)
seasons.notes: Ferrari's first drivers' championship in 21 years.

seasons.engine_formula: 3.0 L naturally aspirated, max 10 cylinders (V10 from 2000 mandated)
seasons.notes: Michelin returned. Traction control legalised again from the Spanish GP.

seasons.engine_formula: 3.0 L naturally aspirated, max 10 cylinders (V10 from 2000 mandated)
seasons.notes: Schumacher finished on the podium in every race — still unmatched. Team orders at the A1-Ring caused such outcry they were banned for 2003.

seasons.engine_formula: 3.0 L naturally aspirated, max 10 cylinders (V10 from 2000 mandated)
seasons.notes: Points widened to the top eight to close the field up; the title went to the last round.

seasons.engine_formula: 3.0 L naturally aspirated, max 10 cylinders (V10 from 2000 mandated)
seasons.notes: Thirteen wins in a season — a record until 2013. Schumacher's fifth straight and seventh overall.

seasons.engine_formula: 3.0 L naturally aspirated, max 10 cylinders (V10 from 2000 mandated)
seasons.notes: Alonso became the youngest champion to that date at 24. Tyre changes were banned; the US GP at Indianapolis was run by six cars after Michelin's tyre failures.

seasons.engine_formula: 3.0 L naturally aspirated, max 10 cylinders (V10 from 2000 mandated)
seasons.notes: Schumacher's first retirement. Last year of V10 engines.

seasons.engine_formula: 2.4 L naturally aspirated V8
seasons.notes: Raikkonen took the title by one point at the final round after McLaren's Hamilton and Alonso split the points. McLaren excluded from the constructors' championship over the 'Spygate' affair and fined $100m.

seasons.engine_formula: 2.4 L naturally aspirated V8
seasons.notes: Decided at the final corner of the final lap in Brazil. Hamilton became the youngest champion at the time and the sport's first Black World Champion.

seasons.engine_formula: 2.4 L naturally aspirated V8
seasons.notes: Brawn GP rose from the collapse of Honda's team and won both titles in its only season, aided by the double-diffuser interpretation. KERS introduced.

seasons.engine_formula: 2.4 L naturally aspirated V8
seasons.notes: Four drivers could win at the finale in Abu Dhabi; Vettel led the championship for the first time only after the last race. Refuelling banned.

seasons.engine_formula: 2.4 L naturally aspirated V8
seasons.notes: Pirelli became sole supplier; DRS and high-degradation tyres introduced to promote overtaking. Vettel took 15 poles.

seasons.engine_formula: 2.4 L naturally aspirated V8
seasons.notes: Seven different winners in the first seven races. Vettel's third straight title by three points.

seasons.engine_formula: 2.4 L naturally aspirated V8
seasons.notes: Nine consecutive wins to end the season — a record. Last year of the V8 era.

seasons.engine_formula: 1.6 L V6 turbo hybrid (ERS: MGU-K + MGU-H)
seasons.notes: The turbo-hybrid era begins. Mercedes won 16 of 19. Double points at the finale (used once, then dropped). Jules Bianchi critically injured at Suzuka.

seasons.engine_formula: 1.6 L V6 turbo hybrid (ERS: MGU-K + MGU-H)
seasons.notes: Hamilton's third title, equalling Senna.

seasons.engine_formula: 1.6 L V6 turbo hybrid (ERS: MGU-K + MGU-H)
seasons.notes: Nico Rosberg won the title and retired five days later. He and Keke are the second father-and-son champions.

seasons.engine_formula: 1.6 L V6 turbo hybrid (ERS: MGU-K + MGU-H)
seasons.notes: Wider cars and tyres brought lap records tumbling. Halo approved for 2018.

seasons.engine_formula: 1.6 L V6 turbo hybrid (ERS: MGU-K + MGU-H)
seasons.notes: Halo introduced. Hamilton's fifth title moved him past Fangio.

seasons.engine_formula: 1.6 L V6 turbo hybrid (ERS: MGU-K + MGU-H)
seasons.notes: Mercedes's sixth consecutive double. Anthoine Hubert killed in the F2 race at Spa.

seasons.engine_formula: 1.6 L V6 turbo hybrid (ERS: MGU-K + MGU-H)
seasons.notes: COVID-shortened calendar with new venues (Mugello, Portimao, Imola, Istanbul, Nurburgring). Hamilton equalled Schumacher's seven titles. Romain Grosjean survived a 67 g fireball at Bahrain.

seasons.engine_formula: 1.6 L V6 turbo hybrid (ERS: MGU-K + MGU-H)
seasons.notes: Settled on the final lap at Abu Dhabi after a contested safety-car restart; the FIA later found the race director had misapplied the rules and restructured race control. Sprint format trialled at three events.

seasons.engine_formula: 1.6 L V6 turbo hybrid (ERS: MGU-K + MGU-H)
seasons.notes: Ground effect returns under new aerodynamic regulations; porpoising dominated the early season. Fifteen wins set a new record.

seasons.engine_formula: 1.6 L V6 turbo hybrid (ERS: MGU-K + MGU-H)
seasons.notes: The most dominant season on record: 19 wins from 22, Red Bull winning 21 of 22 and scoring 860 points.

seasons.engine_formula: 1.6 L V6 turbo hybrid (ERS: MGU-K + MGU-H)
seasons.notes: Verstappen's fourth straight title while McLaren took its first constructors' crown since 1998. Longest calendar to that point at 24 rounds.

seasons.engine_formula: 1.6 L V6 turbo hybrid (ERS: MGU-K + MGU-H)
seasons.notes: Norris beat Verstappen by two points with team-mate Piastri third on 410 — the closest top-three in the sport's history. McLaren's 833 points set a constructors' record. Last season of the 2014-25 power-unit formula.

seasons.engine_formula: 1.6 L V6 turbo hybrid, no MGU-H, ~50/50 ICE/electric split, 100% sustainable fuel
seasons.notes: Season in progress. New chassis and power-unit regulations; Audi and Cadillac join as the 11th and 12th entries. Active aerodynamics replace DRS.

drivers.external_source: formula1.com driver page, 2026-09-04, after round 12 of the 2026 season
drivers.notes: Record holder for wins (105 at end-2025) and poles (104). Equalled Schumacher's seven titles in 2020. Moved to Ferrari for 2025 and took his first Ferrari win at Barcelona in 2026. Start/win totals move with the 2026 season.
Seven titles, five of them consecutive with Ferrari. Held the record for wins (91) until 2020. Suffered a severe brain injury skiing in December 2013.
Five titles with four different constructors — Alfa Romeo, Mercedes, Ferrari and Maserati — a feat never repeated. Won 47% of the races he started, still the highest win rate in the sport.

drivers.external_source: formula1.com driver page, 2026-09-04, after round 12 of the 2026 season
drivers.notes: Youngest ever F1 starter at 17 and youngest winner at 18. Set single-season records for wins (19) and win percentage in 2023. Won 8 of 24 in 2025 but lost the title to Norris by two points.
Youngest ever World Champion at 23 (2010) and youngest four-time champion. Won a record nine consecutive races in 2013.
'The Professor' — won by managing races rather than dominating laps. His rivalry with Senna defined the era. Held the win record (51) from 1987 until Schumacher passed it in 2001.
65 poles from 161 starts. Six Monaco wins including five straight. Killed at Imola on 1 May 1994; the crash triggered the most sweeping safety overhaul in the sport's history.

Three titles, and then a second career as the sport's most consequential safety campaigner — barriers, medical cars, seatbelts, full-face helmets, run-off. Retired one race early after the death of team-mate Cevert.
Survived catastrophic burns at the Nurburgring in 1976 and returned six weeks later. Later non-executive chairman of Mercedes, where he recruited Hamilton.
First champion of the turbo era (1983). Won titles with both Brabham and Williams.
The only driver to win the World Championship in a car of his own construction (1966). Pushed his out-of-fuel Cooper over the line to clinch the 1959 title at Sebring.

drivers.external_source: formula1.com driver page, 2026-09-04, after round 12 of the 2026 season
drivers.notes: Ended Schumacher's run in 2005 as the then-youngest champion. Still racing in 2026 at 45; holds the record for most race starts. Also won Le Mans twice and the WEC title.

Took pole for nearly half his starts. Won the F1 title and the Indianapolis 500 in 1965. Killed in a Formula 2 race at Hockenheim, a death that shook the sport's assumptions about driver invulnerability.
Survived a life-threatening crash at Adelaide in 1995. Senna named him the rival he rated most highly.
Youngest champion for 33 years at 25. Left McLaren at his peak to run the family Copersucar team, then won the Indianapolis 500 twice.
The only driver to complete the Triple Crown: Monaco GP, Indianapolis 500 and Le Mans 24 Hours. Five Monaco wins. Killed piloting his own aircraft in fog near Elstree.

Won nine consecutive championship races across 1952-53, a record that stood until Verstappen in 2023. Killed testing a Ferrari sports car at Monza four days after surviving a plunge into Monaco harbour.
Won the title at the 13th attempt in the Williams FW14B, then left for IndyCar and won that championship as a rookie — the only driver to hold both titles simultaneously.
Beat Hamilton by five points in 2016 and announced his retirement five days later. Son of 1982 champion Keke Rosberg.
Son of Graham Hill; the first second-generation World Champion. Dropped by Williams the year he won the title.
'The Iceman'. Took the 2007 title at the last round by one point. Held the record for most race starts (349) until Alonso passed it.
Won the 2009 title with Brawn GP in the team's only season, after 113 races without a victory.

drivers.external_source: formula1.com driver page, 2026-09-04, after round 12 of the 2026 season
drivers.notes: Waited 110 races for a first win (Miami 2024), then took the 2025 title by two points from Verstappen with team-mate Piastri third — the closest top three in the sport's history.
Delivered Williams its first drivers' title and set the template for the team's uncompromising number-one culture.
Champion in the ground-effect Lotus 79. Also won the Indianapolis 500, the IndyCar title four times and the Daytona 500 — arguably the most versatile record in motorsport.
Son of Gilles Villeneuve. Won the Indianapolis 500 and IndyCar title before arriving in F1 and taking pole on debut at Melbourne.
Took the 1976 title by one point in the Fuji rain. Later a famously unvarnished BBC commentator alongside Murray Walker.
Ferrari's last champion for 21 years. Retired at 30 and became an organic farmer in Hampshire.
'The Bear'. Beat his own employer Jack Brabham to the 1967 title. Died of a heart attack while racing at Bathurst.
The sport's only posthumous World Champion. Killed in practice at Monza; no rival could catch his points total over the remaining four races.
The only World Champion on both two wheels (seven motorcycle world titles) and four. Later ran his own constructor, Team Surtees.
The sport's first World Champion. Already 43 at the first race; killed in a road accident on the way to the 1966 French GP.
Took the 1982 title with a single win in the most turbulent season on record. Father of 2016 champion Nico Rosberg.
Britain's first World Champion, taken with a single win. Retired immediately after the title and was killed in a road crash on the Guildford bypass three months later.
First American World Champion. Took the title at Monza in the race that killed his team-mate von Trips and 15 spectators.
Runner-up four consecutive years (1955-58) and third three times. Universally called the greatest driver never to win the championship.
Runner-up in 2001; the most successful Scottish driver after Clark and Stewart.
Lost the 1981 title to Piquet by a point at the final round. Later governor of Santa Fe province.
Lost the 2008 title by one point at his home race, having crossed the line as champion for 38 seconds. Suffered a fractured skull at the Hungaroring in 2009.
322 starts, a record until Raikkonen. Twice runner-up to Schumacher at Ferrari.
Won for Benetton, Ferrari and McLaren across three decades of regulations. Survived a fiery crash at Imola in 1989.
Twice runner-up. Died of complications after a first-lap crash at Monza, a death that led directly to improved medical response.
Ten wins and four runner-up finishes as Hamilton's Mercedes team-mate. Returned to a race seat with Cadillac in 2026.

drivers.external_source: formula1.com driver page, 2026-09-04, after round 12 of the 2026 season
drivers.notes: Ferrari's lead driver since 2019; won his home Monaco Grand Prix in 2024. Championship runner-up in 2022.
Championship runner-up in 2010; later won the World Endurance Championship with Porsche.

drivers.external_source: formula1.com driver page, 2026-09-04, after round 12 of the 2026 season
drivers.notes: Won seven races in 2025 and finished third, ten points off the title, in the closest top three ever.
Eight wins across Red Bull, Renault and McLaren, several of them from improbable positions.
Twice championship runner-up; six Le Mans wins. Protested the standing Le Mans start by walking to his car.

drivers.external_source: formula1.com driver page, 2026-09-04, after round 12 of the 2026 season
drivers.notes: First win at Interlagos 2022. Won twice in 2025 and again in Australia and Austria in 2026. GPDA director.
Won the Indianapolis 500 and CART title before F1, and passed Schumacher around the outside on his fourth GP start.
His 1979 Dijon duel with Villeneuve is among the most replayed pieces of footage in the sport.
Promoted to Mercedes at 18 to replace Hamilton. Leads the 2026 championship with six wins from the first twelve rounds.
Runner-up in 1979. Killed in qualifying at Zolder. Ferrari has never reissued his number 27 with the same reverence.
Career ended by leg injuries in the 1986 British GP startline crash.
Michael's younger brother; the pair finished 1-2 at the 2001 Canadian GP.
First driver to reach 200 and then 250 Grand Prix starts; runner-up in 1992.
Six wins including Monaco 2022; runner-up in 2023. Returned with Cadillac in 2026.
A dentist by training; runner-up in 1959. Moss rated him the fastest of his contemporaries.
Gave Williams its first Grand Prix win at Silverstone in 1979. Paralysed in a crash at Long Beach in 1980.
Won from 22nd on the grid at Long Beach in 1983 — still the lowest starting position for a winner.
Ferrari's last Italian championship contender, runner-up in 1985. Killed testing an Audi at the Lausitzring.
Youngest GP winner for 44 years (1959 US GP, aged 22). Founded McLaren in 1963; killed testing a Can-Am car at Goodwood.
Won for Ferrari at Silverstone 2022, Singapore 2023 and Melbourne 2024. Son of the double World Rally Champion.
Won a GP in a car of his own construction (Eagle, Spa 1967) — one of only two men to do so. Invented the Gurney flap and the podium champagne spray.
Lost the 1999 title to Hakkinen by two points while deputising for the injured Schumacher.
Leading the 1982 championship when leg injuries at Hockenheim ended his career; killed powerboat racing five years later.
Took Force India's only pole and podium at Spa in 2009.
Championship runner-up in 1997 and third in 1999 with Jordan.
Raced on after career-threatening foot injuries in F3000; later an FIA steward.
Handed his Ferrari to Fangio at Monza in 1956, giving up his own title chance. Killed at the Nurburgring two years later.
All three wins came for Williams in 1989-90, two of them in torrential rain.

Won the Indianapolis 500 in the years it counted towards the Formula One World Championship (1950-1960). Recorded as a World Championship race winner in the official record; did not contest European Grands Prix.
Killed testing at Paul Ricard, where the absence of marshals and medical cover caused an outcry.
Won the first Grand Prix for a turbocharged car, at Dijon in 1979.
Killed in a non-championship race at Brands Hatch.
Gave Ferrari its first World Championship Grand Prix win, at Silverstone in 1951.
Two Monaco wins, eight years apart (1955 and 1958).
Killed testing at Hockenheim.
Took over Villeneuve's Ferrari seat and won at Hockenheim weeks later.
Won for Cooper and BRM; a legendary wet-weather driver.
Killed testing at Kyalami.
Leading the 1961 championship when he was killed at Monza along with 15 spectators.
Won the 1989 Japanese GP after Senna's disqualification; lost an arm in a helicopter crash in 1990 (later reattached).

Won the Indianapolis 500 in the years it counted towards the Formula One World Championship (1950-1960). Recorded as a World Championship race winner in the official record; did not contest European Grands Prix.
Won his home Grand Prix at Interlagos in 1975 for Brabham. Killed in a light-aircraft crash; the Interlagos circuit is named after him.
Won the 2021 Hungarian GP for Alpine.
Stewart's protege and designated successor at Tyrrell; killed in qualifying at Watkins Glen.
The only driver to win on his World Championship debut, the 1961 French Grand Prix at Reims.
Won the 1977 Belgian GP; died of cancer at 29.
Won the 2008 Hungarian GP for McLaren.
Gave Team Lotus its first championship GP win, at Watkins Glen in 1961.
Won Monaco in 2004. The 'Trulli train' entered the sport's vocabulary.
One win in 201 starts — the 1995 Canadian GP, on his birthday, in a Ferrari.
Won the 1972 Monaco Grand Prix for BRM in torrential rain — the team's last victory. Raced with a permanently weakened left arm after a sports-car crash.

Won the Indianapolis 500 in the years it counted towards the Formula One World Championship (1950-1960). Recorded as a World Championship race winner in the official record; did not contest European Grands Prix.

Won the Indianapolis 500 in the years it counted towards the Formula One World Championship (1950-1960). Recorded as a World Championship race winner in the official record; did not contest European Grands Prix.
Gave BRM its first win at Zandvoort in 1959. First chairman of the Grand Prix Drivers' Association.
Won the shortened 1975 Spanish GP at Montjuic, stopped after a fatal accident.

constructors.name: Ferrari
constructors.notes: The only constructor to have contested every season since 1950. Fifteen drivers' titles and sixteen constructors' titles, the last in 2008. Won its first championship Grand Prix at Silverstone in 1951 with Gonzalez.

constructors.name: McLaren
constructors.notes: Founded by Bruce McLaren in 1963, first entry 1966. Second only to Ferrari in wins and titles. The MP4/4 of 1988 won 15 of 16 races. Returned to the top in 2024-25 after a 26-year constructors' drought.

constructors.name: Williams
constructors.notes: Frank Williams's second and lasting venture. Nine constructors' titles, all between 1980 and 1997. Sold to Dorilton Capital in 2020, ending family control.

constructors.name: Mercedes
constructors.notes: Two spells: a works team in 1954-55 that won two titles with Fangio and withdrew after Le Mans, and the modern operation that took over Brawn GP in 2010 and won eight consecutive constructors' championships from 2014. Registered first entry 1954; the current entity traces its entry chain through BAR and Honda.

constructors.name: Team Lotus
constructors.notes: Colin Chapman's constructor: the monocoque chassis (Lotus 25), full ground effect (Lotus 78/79), active suspension and the first major commercial sponsorship deal. Collapsed in 1994 after Chapman's death in 1982.

constructors.name: Red Bull Racing
constructors.notes: Bought the Jaguar entry for a nominal sum in late 2004. Six constructors' titles and eight drivers' titles in twenty seasons. Its 2023 season — 21 wins from 22 — is the most dominant in the sport's history.

constructors.name: Brabham
constructors.notes: Founded by Jack Brabham and Ron Tauranac. Later run by Bernie Ecclestone, whose ownership was the platform for his takeover of the sport's commercial rights. The BT46B 'fan car' won its only race and was withdrawn.

constructors.name: Cooper
constructors.notes: Put the engine behind the driver and made the front-engined Grand Prix car obsolete within three seasons.

constructors.name: Renault
constructors.notes: Introduced the turbocharged engine to F1 in 1977 and won two doubles with Alonso in 2005-06 after buying Benetton. Withdrew as a works entrant at the end of 2020, rebranding as Alpine.

constructors.name: BRM
constructors.notes: A national-effort project that took eleven years to win a championship. Built the extraordinary H16 engine.

constructors.name: Benetton
constructors.notes: Bought Toleman in 1985. Michael Schumacher's first two titles came here; the team's 1994 season was dogged by technical-compliance disputes.

constructors.name: Brawn GP
constructors.notes: Ross Brawn's management buyout of Honda's abandoned team for a nominal sum. Won both championships in its only season and was sold to Mercedes.

constructors.name: Matra
constructors.notes: An aerospace company that won the title at its third attempt, run in 1969 by Ken Tyrrell with Ford power.

constructors.name: Tyrrell
constructors.notes: Ken Tyrrell's team, which built the six-wheeled P34. Sold to British American Tobacco in 1997 and became BAR.

constructors.name: Vanwall
constructors.notes: Tony Vandervell's team won the first Constructors' Championship in 1958 and withdrew almost immediately after Stuart Lewis-Evans's death.

constructors.name: Alfa Romeo
constructors.notes: Dominated 1950-51 with the pre-war 158/159 'Alfetta' and won the first two drivers' titles, then withdrew. Returned as a constructor 1979-85 and later as a naming-rights partner to Sauber, 2019-2023.

constructors.name: Alpine
constructors.notes: The Renault works entry rebadged for 2021. One win, at the 2021 Hungarian GP with Ocon. The Enstone factory it occupies has won two constructors' titles under earlier names.

constructors.name: Arrows
constructors.notes: 382 starts without a win — the most of any constructor. Came closest with Damon Hill at the Hungaroring in 1997.

constructors.name: Aston Martin
constructors.full_name: Aston Martin Aramco Formula One Team
constructors.notes: Two spells. Aston Martin entered the front-engined DBR4 and DBR5 in 1959-60, by which time the rear-engined Coopers had made them obsolete; the marque scored no points. The current entity is unrelated, dating from Lawrence Stroll's 2021 rebrand of Racing Point. Adrian Newey joined as team principal for 2026.

constructors.name: Audi
constructors.notes: The Hinwil operation founded by Peter Sauber, taken over completely by Audi for the 2026 regulations. Audi builds its own power unit at Neuburg an der Donau — the first new works manufacturer entry since Honda's return.

constructors.name: BMW Sauber
constructors.notes: BMW's works entry, second in the 2007 constructors' championship. Withdrew after 2009.

constructors.name: British American Racing
constructors.notes: Built from the Tyrrell entry with British American Tobacco money. Second in the 2004 constructors' championship.

constructors.name: Cadillac
constructors.notes: The eleventh team, admitted for 2026 after a protracted approval process originally begun as the Andretti-Cadillac bid. Runs Ferrari power units pending its own General Motors unit.

constructors.name: Caterham / Team Lotus (2010-14)
constructors.notes: Entered as Lotus Racing, raced as Team Lotus in 2011 amid a naming dispute with the Enstone team, then as Caterham. Never scored.

constructors.name: Connaught
constructors.notes: British constructor whose Type B gave Britain one of its first significant Grand Prix results at Syracuse in 1955.

constructors.name: Dallara
constructors.notes: Better known now as a supplier of chassis to other series; ran its own Formula One entry through Scuderia Italia, taking two podiums.

constructors.name: Eagle
constructors.notes: Dan Gurney won the 1967 Belgian GP in a car of his own construction — one of only two men to do so.

constructors.name: Fittipaldi
constructors.notes: Emerson Fittipaldi left McLaren as a double champion to drive for his brother Wilson's team. It never won a race and the decision is usually read as the one that ended his career at the front.

constructors.name: Footwork
constructors.notes: Arrows under its Japanese owner's name from 1991 to 1996. Held here as a separate register entry because that is how the results were published; it is the same operation as Arrows.

constructors.name: Force India
constructors.notes: Vijay Mallya's team took pole and a podium at Spa in 2009 and finished fourth in 2016 and 2017 before going into administration.

constructors.name: Gordini
constructors.notes: Amedee Gordini's small team, chronically underfunded and known as 'le sorcier' for extracting results from very little money.

constructors.name: HRT
constructors.notes: One of the three 2010 entrants admitted on the promise of a budget cap that never arrived. Never scored a point.

constructors.name: Haas F1 Team
constructors.notes: The first American constructor since 1986, and the first to run a customer-parts model built around Ferrari supply and Dallara manufacture.

constructors.name: Hesketh
constructors.notes: Lord Hesketh's unsponsored team won the 1975 Dutch GP with James Hunt.

constructors.name: Honda
constructors.notes: Two spells as a constructor: 1964-68, winning in Mexico 1965 and Monza 1967, and 2006-08 after buying BAR. Withdrew in the 2008 financial crisis, whereupon the team became Brawn GP.

constructors.name: Jaguar Racing
constructors.notes: Ford's rebadging of Stewart. Never won a race; sold to Red Bull for a nominal sum in 2004.

constructors.name: Jordan
constructors.notes: Eddie Jordan's team gave Michael Schumacher his F1 debut at Spa in 1991 and finished third in the 1999 championship.

constructors.name: Lancia
constructors.notes: The D50 was handed to Ferrari after Ascari's death and won the 1956 title in Fangio's hands as the Lancia-Ferrari.

constructors.name: Larrousse
constructors.notes: Gerard Larrousse's team, which took a surprise podium at Suzuka in 1990 with Aguri Suzuki - the first by a Japanese driver.

constructors.name: Leyton House
constructors.notes: The renamed March team, running Adrian Newey's designs. Ivan Capelli led the 1990 French Grand Prix until nine laps from the end.

constructors.name: Ligier
constructors.notes: Guy Ligier's team; sold to Alain Prost in 1997.

constructors.name: Lola
constructors.notes: Eric Broadley's constructor, better known for sports and Indycars. Its 1962 Formula One car was run by the Bowmaker team for John Surtees, and the Lola name reappeared as a chassis supplier for decades afterwards.

constructors.name: Lotus F1 Team
constructors.notes: The Enstone team under Genii Capital ownership, using the Lotus name by licence. Raikkonen won in Abu Dhabi 2012 and Australia 2013.

constructors.name: March
constructors.notes: A customer-car manufacturer that also ran a works entry; Peterson and Lauda both started here.

constructors.name: Maserati
constructors.notes: The 250F is among the most admired Grand Prix cars ever built; Fangio took the 1957 title in one.

constructors.name: Minardi
constructors.notes: The Faenza team's original identity; a proving ground for Alonso, Trulli, Fisichella and Webber. Sold to Red Bull in 2005.

constructors.name: Onyx
constructors.notes: Lasted a season and a half and took one podium, Johansson's third at Estoril in 1989.

constructors.name: Penske
constructors.notes: Won the 1976 Austrian GP with John Watson, then left for American racing. The PC4 raced on into 1977 in other hands - ATS Racing and Interscope - which is why the constructor's last entry is a year after the team's.

constructors.name: Porsche
constructors.notes: Won the 1962 French GP with Dan Gurney. Returned as an engine supplier badged TAG in the 1980s.

constructors.name: Prost Grand Prix
constructors.notes: Alain Prost's purchase of Ligier; collapsed in bankruptcy in 2002.

constructors.name: Racing Bulls
constructors.full_name: Visa Cash App Racing Bulls Formula One Team
constructors.notes: The Faenza entry, continuously in the championship since Minardi's 1985 debut. Two wins, both giant-killings: Vettel at Monza in 2008 and Gasly at Monza in 2020. The Faenza team's two wins are credited to the constructor names it raced under at the time, Toro Rosso (2008) and AlphaTauri (2020).

constructors.name: Racing Point
constructors.notes: Won the 2020 Sakhir GP with Perez. Penalised that year for copying Mercedes brake ducts — the 'pink Mercedes' affair.

constructors.name: Rob Walker Racing
constructors.notes: The most successful private entrant in history: Moss's 1958 Argentine GP win was the first for a mid-engined car and the first for a privateer. Its Grand Prix victories are credited to the Cooper and Lotus chassis it entered, so it holds no constructor win total of its own.

constructors.name: Sauber
constructors.notes: Peter Sauber's independent team. Its single win came as BMW Sauber with Kubica in Canada 2008. Ran as Alfa Romeo 2019-23 and Kick Sauber 2024-25 before becoming Audi. Its single victory is credited to BMW Sauber, the constructor name in use in 2008.

constructors.name: Scuderia AlphaTauri
constructors.notes: The Faenza team rebranded to promote Red Bull's fashion label. Gasly won at Monza in 2020.

constructors.name: Scuderia Toro Rosso
constructors.notes: Red Bull's junior team; Vettel's Monza 2008 win remains the last for a team using a customer chassis philosophy of that kind.

constructors.name: Shadow
constructors.notes: Won the 1977 Austrian GP with Alan Jones. A staff walkout founded Arrows.

constructors.name: Stewart Grand Prix
constructors.notes: Jackie and Paul Stewart's Ford-backed team won at the Nurburgring in 1999 and was sold to Ford to become Jaguar.

constructors.name: Super Aguri
constructors.notes: Aguri Suzuki's Honda-backed team; scored a point at Montreal in 2007 and folded mid-2008.

constructors.name: Surtees
constructors.notes: John Surtees's own constructor.

constructors.name: Talbot-Lago
constructors.notes: Ran the pre-war T26C through the early 1950s. Its naturally aspirated 4.5-litre engine was slower than the supercharged Alfas but drank far less, so a Talbot could sometimes run a race non-stop while the front-runners refuelled twice. Rosier won Spa in 1950 that way.

constructors.name: Toleman
constructors.notes: Ayrton Senna's first team; his second place in the Monaco rain of 1984 announced him. Sold to Benetton.

constructors.name: Toyota
constructors.notes: The largest budget in the sport for much of its run and no wins from 139 starts. Withdrew after 2009.

constructors.name: Virgin Racing / Marussia / Manor
constructors.notes: Ran as Virgin, Marussia and Manor. Jules Bianchi's ninth place at Monaco in 2014 was its only points finish; he was fatally injured at Suzuka that year.

constructors.name: Walter Wolf Racing
constructors.notes: Won on its championship debut in Argentina 1977 with Scheckter — a feat matched only by Brawn GP.

engine_manufacturers.name: Ferrari
engine_manufacturers.notes: The only manufacturer present for every season. Supplies Haas and Cadillac as well as the works team in 2026.

engine_manufacturers.name: Alfa Romeo
engine_manufacturers.notes: The supercharged 158/159 straight-eight won the first two titles.

engine_manufacturers.name: Maserati
engine_manufacturers.notes: Powered Fangio's 1957 title in the 250F.

engine_manufacturers.name: BRM
engine_manufacturers.notes: Built the 1.5 L V8 that won the 1962 title and the notoriously complex H16.

engine_manufacturers.name: Coventry Climax
engine_manufacturers.notes: A fire-pump engine manufacturer whose FPF and FWMV engines powered Cooper and Lotus to championships.

engine_manufacturers.name: Mercedes
engine_manufacturers.notes: Dominated the first turbo-hybrid years with a split-turbo layout that rivals took three seasons to match. Supplies McLaren, Williams and Alpine in 2026.

engine_manufacturers.name: Honda
engine_manufacturers.notes: Four distinct eras: works constructor 1964-68, supplier to Williams and McLaren 1983-92, 2000s works entry, and the 2015- return that powered Verstappen's four titles. Badged HRC and supplying Aston Martin in 2026.

engine_manufacturers.name: Repco
engine_manufacturers.notes: An Australian parts company whose lightweight V8 won two titles for Brabham in the first years of the 3.0 L formula.

engine_manufacturers.name: Weslake
engine_manufacturers.notes: Powered Gurney's Eagle to victory at Spa in 1967.

engine_manufacturers.name: Ford Cosworth
engine_manufacturers.notes: The DFV, funded by Ford for £100,000, won on debut at Zandvoort in 1967 and 155 Grands Prix in all. It made the customer-chassis garagiste team viable and defined F1 for two decades.

engine_manufacturers.name: Matra
engine_manufacturers.notes: The V12 was slow but its sound is among the most celebrated in the sport.

engine_manufacturers.name: Renault
engine_manufacturers.notes: Introduced the turbo to F1 in 1977 and powered Williams, Benetton and Red Bull to titles as a supplier. Withdrew from power-unit supply after 2024.

engine_manufacturers.name: Hart
engine_manufacturers.notes: Brian Hart's independent engines, used by Toleman, Jordan and Arrows.

engine_manufacturers.name: BMW
engine_manufacturers.notes: The M12/13 four-cylinder turbo, derived from a production block, is credited with over 1,400 bhp in qualifying trim in 1986 — the highest figure ever run in F1.

engine_manufacturers.name: TAG (Porsche)
engine_manufacturers.notes: Porsche-built, TAG-funded turbo V6 that powered McLaren to three drivers' and two constructors' titles.

engine_manufacturers.name: Judd
engine_manufacturers.notes: An independent customer supplier of the late 1980s.

engine_manufacturers.name: Yamaha
engine_manufacturers.notes: Never won; came closest with Damon Hill's Arrows at the 1997 Hungarian GP.

engine_manufacturers.name: Mugen-Honda
engine_manufacturers.notes: A Honda-derived independent that won with Ligier and Jordan.

engine_manufacturers.name: Peugeot
engine_manufacturers.notes: Supplied McLaren, Jordan and Prost without a win.

engine_manufacturers.name: Toyota
engine_manufacturers.notes: Supplied its own team plus Williams; no wins.

engine_manufacturers.name: Red Bull Powertrains
engine_manufacturers.notes: Created when Honda withdrew as a badged supplier; from 2026 a full in-house power unit developed with Ford.

engine_manufacturers.name: Audi
engine_manufacturers.notes: Designed and built at Neuburg an der Donau — the first all-new works manufacturer power unit of the 2026 formula.

engine_eras.formula: 1.5 L supercharged or 4.5 L naturally aspirated
engine_eras.notes: Pre-war technology carried into the new championship. Alfa's 159 used around 125 litres of fuel per 100 km.
Adopted because too few F1 cars remained after Alfa Romeo's withdrawal.
Mercedes's desmodromic-valve W196 and the Maserati 250F belong to this period; ends with the rear-engine revolution.
Unpopular on introduction for cutting power, but produced light, nimble cars and Clark's Lotus 25 monocoque.

engine_eras.formula: 3.0 L naturally aspirated or 1.5 L forced induction
engine_eras.notes: The Cosworth DFV arrived in 1967 and made the independent constructor viable.

engine_eras.formula: 3.0 L naturally aspirated or 1.5 L turbocharged
engine_eras.notes: Renault's RS01 introduced turbocharging in 1977. Qualifying boost produced the highest power outputs in the sport's history before boost limits (4.0 bar in 1987, 2.5 bar in 1988) closed the era.
Turbos banned outright. The V10 emerged as the best compromise between the V8's weight and the V12's power.
Capacity cut for safety after 1994. By 2005 the best engines revved past 19,000 rpm and lasted two race weekends.
Rev limits and long-life rules progressively froze development. KERS introduced in 2009.
Thermal efficiency passed 50% — roughly double a road engine. Mercedes's split-turbo layout, with compressor and turbine at opposite ends of the engine, gave it a multi-year advantage.

engine_eras.formula: 1.6 L V6 turbo hybrid, no MGU-H
engine_eras.notes: MGU-H removed to cut cost and complexity and to attract new manufacturers; electrical power raised to around 350 kW; 100% advanced sustainable fuel mandated. Audi, Ford (with Red Bull) and Cadillac's forthcoming GM unit were all drawn in by this ruleset.

cars.designers: Mauro Forghieri
cars.chassis_type: steel tube frame with aluminium shear panels
cars.suspension: Front and rear double wishbone, front inboard spring/damper
cars.concept: Turn the gearbox sideways and put it ahead of the rear axle line: the mass moves forward and the car turns better
cars.innovations: The transverse gearbox - the T in the name is trasversale - which concentrated mass within the wheelbase
cars.story: The 312T line ran for six seasons and five designations and is the most successful thing Ferrari built before the Schumacher era. The 312T2 is the car Lauda crashed at the Nurburgring in 1976 and the car he was back in six weeks later. By the 312T5 in 1980 the flat-12 was too wide for ground effect and the car was hopeless - Ferrari finished tenth in the championship, and went turbo.
cars.outcome: 89 races, 27 wins, 19 poles. Drivers' titles for Lauda (1975, 1977) and Scheckter (1979); constructors' in 1975, 1976, 1977 and 1979.

cars.designers: Adrian Newey, Pierre Wache, Craig Skinner, Enrico Balbo
cars.suspension: Pushrod front, pullrod rear, with carbon-composite wishbones
cars.concept: The most complete exploitation of the 2022 ground-effect rules: low drag on the straights without giving anything up in the corners
cars.story: Twenty-one wins from twenty-two races, beating the MP4/4's 93.8 per cent with 95.5 per cent, and leading 86.7 per cent of all laps run. The one it lost was Singapore. Verstappen won ten in a row, a record. It is the most dominant single season any car has had, and it happened under a cost cap that was supposed to prevent exactly this.
cars.outcome: 22 races, 21 wins. Verstappen's third title and Red Bull's sixth constructors' championship.

cars.designers: Patrick Head, Adrian Newey, Paddy Lowe, Frank Dernie
cars.suspension: Pushrod with inboard spring/dampers in 1991; computer-controlled active suspension front and rear on the 1992 FW14B
cars.concept: Give the computer control of the ride height and the car holds its best aerodynamic attitude everywhere, all the time
cars.innovations: Active suspension, traction control, semi-automatic gearbox and anti-lock brakes on one car
cars.story: The FW14B is the most technologically advanced car ever to race in Formula One, and it is the reason so much of it is now banned. Mansell won the first five races of 1992 and took the title with five rounds left. Active suspension, traction control and launch control were all outlawed for 1994, which is how a technical arms race ends.
cars.outcome: 17 wins and 21 poles across the two years. Mansell's 1992 title with nine wins in a season, and the 1992 constructors' championship.

cars.designers: Bob Bell, Aldo Costa, Geoff Willis, John Owen, Mike Elliott, Loic Serra
cars.power_note: About 840 bhp combined at up to 15,000 rpm, from a 1.6-litre V6 plus MGU-K and MGU-H
cars.chassis_type: moulded carbon-fibre and honeycomb composite monocoque
cars.suspension: Carbon-fibre wishbones, pushrod front and pullrod rear, actuating torsion springs
cars.concept: Split the turbocharger in half and put the compressor at the front of the V and the turbine at the back, joined by a shaft through the vee
cars.innovations: The split-turbo layout, which shortened the intake path, cooled the charge air better and packaged the whole power unit tighter than anything else on the grid
cars.story: The 2014 hybrid rules were the biggest engine change since 1989 and Mercedes had understood them years earlier. The split turbo is the single decision that bought them the next eight constructors' championships: Ferrari and Renault had to redesign around it and were years catching up. Hamilton and Rosberg won 16 of 19 races and finished first and second in the championship.
cars.outcome: 19 races, 16 wins, 18 poles. Hamilton's second title and the first of eight consecutive Mercedes constructors' championships.

cars.designers: Gordon Murray, Steve Nichols, Matthew Jeffreys, Bob Bell
cars.power_note: 675 bhp at 12,500 rpm, restricted to 2.5 bar boost and 150 litres of fuel by the 1988 rules
cars.suspension: Front: double wishbones, pull/push-rod actuated coil springs and dampers. Rear: double wishbones, rocker-arm actuated
cars.concept: Murray's very low Brabham packaging, Honda's last and best turbo, and the two fastest drivers alive
cars.story: In the final year of turbos, with boost and fuel cut hard, McLaren won 15 of 16 races and led 1,003 of 1,031 laps. The one it lost was Monza, two laps from the end, when Senna hit a backmarker while leading - five weeks after Enzo Ferrari's death, and Ferrari finished first and second. Senna and Prost took 199 of a possible 240 points between them and did not speak civilly again for years.
cars.outcome: 15 wins, 15 poles and 10 fastest laps from 16 races. Senna's first title and McLaren's constructors' championship.

cars.designers: Ross Brawn, Rory Byrne, Aldo Costa, John Iley, Paolo Martinelli
cars.power_note: 865 bhp at 18,300 rpm in race trim; 900-940 bhp at 19,000 rpm in qualifying
cars.suspension: Independent front and rear, pushrod-activated torsion springs
cars.concept: The last and best of the V10s, at the end of five years of Ferrari getting everything slightly more right than everyone else
cars.story: The F2004 still holds outright lap records at circuits that have not been reprofiled since, which is a strange thing to be able to say about a car from 2004 - modern cars are heavier, on worse tyres, with less engine. It was the end of the run: Schumacher's seventh title, Ferrari's sixth straight constructors' championship, and then the tyre rules changed and it stopped.
cars.outcome: 20 races, 15 wins, 12 poles, 14 fastest laps. Schumacher's seventh drivers' title and Ferrari's 2004 constructors' championship.

cars.designers: James Allison, John Owen, Mike Elliott, Loic Serra, Eric Blandin
cars.engine_name: Mercedes-Benz M11 EQ Performance turbo V6
cars.power_note: Around 1,000 bhp combined, the peak of the first hybrid formula
cars.chassis_type: moulded carbon-fibre and honeycomb composite monocoque
cars.suspension: Carbon-fibre wishbones with pushrod front and pullrod rear, plus Dual Axis Steering
cars.concept: Let the driver change the front wheel toe angle by pulling the steering wheel towards him on the straights
cars.innovations: Dual Axis Steering (DAS), which traded straight-line drag against cornering grip and tyre warm-up within a lap
cars.story: DAS was spotted on television during pre-season testing, ruled legal for 2020 and banned for 2021 in the same breath. The W11 won 13 of 17 races in a season compressed and reordered by the pandemic, and holds the outright lap record at most circuits it visited.
cars.outcome: 17 races, 13 wins, 15 poles. Hamilton's seventh title, equalling Schumacher, and Mercedes's seventh consecutive constructors' championship.

cars.designers: Colin Chapman, Maurice Philippe, Tony Rudd
cars.suspension: Front: double wishbone, inboard spring/damper. Rear: parallel top links, lower wishbones, twin radius arms, outboard spring/damper
cars.concept: Move the mass to the middle, get the radiators out of the nose, and make the whole car a wedge
cars.innovations: Side-mounted radiators in the sidepods, freeing the nose to be a pure aerodynamic wedge; inboard brakes to cut unsprung weight; torsion-bar suspension with anti-dive and anti-squat geometry
cars.story: Twelve miles an hour quicker than the 49 on the same engine. The 72 raced for six seasons, which nothing else of its era managed, and it won the 1970 title for a driver who had died at Monza with four rounds to go - Rindt remains the only posthumous World Champion.
cars.outcome: 75 races, 20 wins, 17 poles. Drivers' titles for Rindt (1970) and Fittipaldi (1972); constructors' in 1970, 1972 and 1973.

cars.designers: Gioacchino Colombo
cars.power_note: Over 300 bhp as the 158 in 1950; about 420 bhp at 9,600 rpm as the 159 in 1951
cars.suspension: Front: trailing arm, transverse leaf springs. Rear: swing axle with transverse leaf spring, replaced by a de Dion axle on the 159
cars.concept: A pre-war voiturette design, hidden through the war and brought back to win the first two World Championships
cars.innovations: Nothing new: the point of the 158 is that a 1938 design was still the best car in the world in 1951
cars.story: Alfa entered 1950 with a car designed twelve years earlier and won every race it started. By 1951 it was drinking fuel at about 1.5 miles per gallon and needed two stops where the Ferrari 375 needed one; Fangio won the title anyway, at Barcelona, when Ferrari picked the wrong tyre size. Alfa then withdrew from Grand Prix racing entirely rather than build a successor, which is why 1952 and 1953 were run to Formula Two rules.
cars.outcome: Every race entered in 1950; 4 of 7 in 1951. Drivers' titles for Farina and Fangio.

cars.designers: Patrick Head, Neil Oatley, Frank Dernie
cars.power_note: 500-510 bhp at 11,400 rpm with the Judd-prepared DFVs from 1980
cars.suspension: Lower wishbones with inboard springs front and rear
cars.concept: The Lotus 79 concept, engineered properly and made stiff enough to hold its skirts on the ground
cars.innovations: Dernie's work on keeping the skirts sealed at all times, worth a claimed 30 per cent in downforce
cars.story: Williams took the 79's idea and out-built its inventor. The FW07 turned a team that had never won a race into a two-time constructors' champion in three seasons and set the pattern for Williams for the next twenty years: someone else's concept, executed better.
cars.outcome: 43 races, 15 wins, 8 poles. Jones's 1980 drivers' title; constructors' championships in 1980 and 1981.

cars.designers: Rudolf Uhlenhaut
cars.power_note: 257 bhp on debut, developed towards 290-300 bhp; a 340 bhp target at 10,000 rpm was never reached in a race
cars.suspension: Front: double wishbone with torsion bars. Rear: low-pivot swing axle with torsion bars
cars.concept: Aircraft engineering applied to a racing car: direct fuel injection, desmodromic valves, and a full-width streamliner body
cars.innovations: Direct fuel injection taken from Daimler-Benz aero engines; desmodromic valve gear, which closes the valves mechanically instead of with springs and so removes the rev ceiling that valve float imposes; inboard brakes; the Type Monza streamliner
cars.story: The only closed-wheel car ever to win a World Championship race, and it won three. Mercedes ran the streamliner at fast circuits and an open-wheel body elsewhere after Fangio complained he could not place the front wheels at Silverstone. The programme ended abruptly after Le Mans 1955, where a Mercedes sports car went into the crowd and killed more than eighty people; Mercedes did not return to Formula One as a constructor until 2010.
cars.outcome: 9 wins from 12 races entered. Fangio's titles in 1954 and 1955.

cars.designers: Colin Chapman (chassis), Frank Costin (aerodynamics), Leo Kuzmicki (engine)
cars.power_note: About 290 bhp at 7,500 rpm on methanol; 255-262 bhp under the 1958 pump-fuel rules
cars.suspension: Front: torsion bars. Rear: de Dion axle
cars.concept: A motorcycle engine multiplied by four in an aircraft-aerodynamicist's body on a Chapman chassis
cars.innovations: Bosch fuel injection; Costin's streamlined body, which made it the fastest car in a straight line; four cylinders derived from Norton motorcycle practice
cars.story: Tony Vandervell built Vanwall to beat 'those bloody red cars', and did. The 1957 British Grand Prix, shared by Moss and Brooks, was the first World Championship win for a British car. In 1958 Vanwall took the first Constructors' Championship ever awarded - and then Vandervell's health failed and the team effectively stopped, so the first constructors' champion never defended the title.
cars.outcome: The first Constructors' Championship, 1958. Six wins that season, three each to Moss and Brooks - and no drivers' title, which went to Hawthorn's Ferrari on consistency.

cars.designers: Adrian Newey, Rob Marshall, Peter Prodromou, Dan Fallows
cars.power_note: 750 bhp at 18,000 rpm, the regulation rev limit
cars.chassis_type: carbon-fibre and honeycomb composite monocoque, engine a fully stressed member
cars.suspension: Aluminium uprights with carbon-composite double wishbones; pushrod front, pullrod rear
cars.concept: Point the exhausts into the diffuser so the car makes downforce from engine gas as well as airflow
cars.innovations: The exhaust-blown diffuser, taken further than anyone else and eventually to off-throttle blowing, which kept the effect alive when the driver lifted
cars.story: Fifteen poles from nineteen races - the car was on another level over one lap and merely very good over a race distance. Vettel took the championship at the last round in Abu Dhabi having led the standings for exactly none of the season until it ended. Exhaust blowing was progressively restricted and then banned for 2014.
cars.outcome: 19 races, 9 wins, 15 poles. Vettel's first title and Red Bull's first constructors' championship.

cars.designers: Mauro Forghieri
cars.suspension: Front: double wishbone, inboard spring/damper. Rear: double wishbone
cars.concept: A flat-12 sits low, so the centre of gravity sits low, and the engine can still be a stressed member
cars.innovations: The 180-degree flat-12 that Ferrari would use until turbos arrived in 1980
cars.story: Forghieri's flat-12 was the answer to the DFV: more power, and mounted so low that it lowered the whole car around it. Its drawback was width, which fought the ground-effect sidepods that arrived at the end of the decade - the reason Ferrari struggled in 1979-80 while Williams and Lotus flew.
cars.outcome: 10 wins across the 312B, B2 and B3. The B3-74 took Lauda to the 1975 title and Ferrari to the constructors'.

cars.designers: Bob Bell, Pat Symonds, James Allison, Tim Densham, Dino Toso
cars.suspension: Pushrod-activated torsion bars front and rear, plus a tuned mass damper in the nose from late 2005
cars.concept: A well-balanced car on Michelins, plus a weight on a spring in the nose to stop the front tyres skipping over bumps
cars.innovations: The tuned mass damper: a sprung mass in the nose oscillating out of phase with the front suspension, keeping the tyres in contact with the road
cars.story: The mass damper was worth about three tenths of a second and was completely legal until the FIA decided in 2006 that a mass that is not rigidly attached counts as a movable aerodynamic device. Renault won the 2005 titles and broke a run of five consecutive Ferrari championships doing it.
cars.outcome: 19 races, 8 wins, 7 poles. Alonso's first title, at 24 the youngest champion to that point, and Renault's first constructors' championship.

cars.designers: Ross Brawn, Jorg Zander, Loic Bigois, John Owen, Masayuki Minagawa (double diffuser)
cars.power_note: 750 bhp at 18,000 rpm, the regulation rev limit
cars.chassis_type: moulded carbon-fibre and honeycomb composite monocoque
cars.suspension: Wishbone and pushrod-activated torsion springs and rockers, front and rear
cars.concept: Read the 2009 aerodynamic rewrite more carefully than anyone else and find a second deck in the diffuser that the wording does not forbid
cars.innovations: The double diffuser, developed at Honda and inherited when Honda withdrew
cars.story: Honda spent a fortune on the 2009 car and then pulled out of Formula One in December 2008. Brawn bought the team for a pound, fitted a Mercedes engine to a chassis designed around a Honda one, and won six of the first seven races. Rivals protested the diffuser and lost at the FIA International Court of Appeal in April. It is the only team to have won the championship in the only season it ever existed - Mercedes bought it at the end of the year.
cars.outcome: 17 races, 8 wins, 5 poles. Button's title and the constructors' championship, from a team that did not exist in January and did not exist in the following year.

cars.designers: Colin Chapman
cars.suspension: Front: double wishbone, inboard coilover. Rear: lower wishbone, top link and radius rod, outboard coilover
cars.concept: Replace the tube frame with a stressed aluminium skin: half the weight, three times the stiffness
cars.innovations: The first fully stressed monocoque chassis in Formula One, and an extremely low, narrow body around a reclined driving position
cars.story: Chapman is said to have sketched it on a napkin. The spaceframe it replaced was a lattice of tubes that had to be triangulated around the driver; the monocoque made the driver's compartment itself the structure. Frontal area came down to 8 square feet. Every serious Formula One car since has been a monocoque of one material or another, and the 25 is the reason.
cars.outcome: 14 wins and 14 poles. Clark's 1963 and 1965 titles, with Lotus taking the constructors' championship both years.

cars.designers: Gordon Coppuck, John Barnard, Dave Quill
cars.suspension: Front: double wishbone with inboard coilovers. Rear: double wishbone
cars.concept: A deformable-structure chassis built to the new 1973 safety rules, developed for six years without ever being replaced
cars.story: The M23 won titles three years apart with two different drivers and was still scoring points in its sixth season. Hunt's 1976 championship in it - won by a point after Lauda's Nurburgring crash and withdrawal at a flooded Fuji - is the season most people who do not follow the sport have still heard of.
cars.outcome: 83 races, 16 wins, 14 poles. Fittipaldi's 1974 title and McLaren's first constructors' championship, then Hunt's 1976 title.

cars.designers: Gioacchino Colombo, Vittorio Bellentani, Alberto Massimino
cars.power_note: 220 bhp at 7,400 rpm in 1954, about 240 bhp with fuel injection from 1955; a 315 bhp V12 was offered in 1957 and rarely used
cars.suspension: Front: independent wishbone. Rear: de Dion tube
cars.concept: The customer car of the 2.5-litre era: not the fastest, but the one anyone could buy and almost anyone could drive
cars.story: The 250F is the reason the mid-1950s grids existed at all - Maserati sold them to privateers and they filled out every race for six seasons. Fangio's 1957 German Grand Prix in one is the drive the sport keeps coming back to: a botched pit stop dropped him 48 seconds behind, and he took it all back in 22 laps, breaking the lap record ten times and passing Hawthorn on the last lap.
cars.outcome: 8 championship wins across 1954-1960. Fangio's 1954 and 1957 titles.

cars.designers: Owen Maddock
cars.suspension: Front: double wishbone, coil spring and damper. Rear: transverse leaf spring with double wishbone
cars.concept: Put the engine behind the driver and the whole car gets smaller, lighter and faster with less power
cars.innovations: Not the first rear-engined Grand Prix car, but the one that settled the argument
cars.story: Cooper's rear-engined cars had been winning with half the power of a front-engined Ferrari since 1958, and the establishment kept explaining why it did not matter. Brabham's 1959 title ended the discussion: within three seasons every car on the grid had the engine behind the driver, and no front-engined car has won a World Championship race since 1960.
cars.outcome: 5 wins. Brabham's 1959 drivers' title and Cooper's 1959 constructors' title - the first for a rear-engined car.

cars.designers: Colin Chapman, Maurice Philippe
cars.power_note: 420-440 bhp at 9,000-10,000 rpm through its life
cars.suspension: Front: double wishbone with inboard spring/damper. Rear: top link, lower wishbone and radius rods
cars.concept: Bolt the engine straight to the back of the tub and let it be the back of the car
cars.innovations: The engine as a fully stressed structural member, carrying the rear suspension; and, from 1968, aerofoil wings mounted on struts to the uprights
cars.story: Ford paid Cosworth £100,000 to build the DFV and gave Lotus a year of exclusivity. Clark won first time out at Zandvoort. When the exclusivity lapsed the DFV was sold to anyone who asked, and it went on to win 155 Grands Prix - the reason a small British team with no engine of its own could beat Ferrari for the next fifteen years. The 49 also carried the first wings, which appeared at Monaco in 1968 and were mounted so high and so flimsily that two of them collapsed at Montjuic in 1969.
cars.outcome: 12 wins, 19 poles. Hill's 1968 title and Rindt's posthumous 1970 title.

cars.designers: Colin Chapman, Tony Rudd, Ralph Bellamy, Peter Wright, Martin Ogilvie
cars.suspension: Front: double wishbone, inboard spring/damper. Rear: parallel top links, lower wishbones, twin radius arms
cars.concept: Shape the underside of the sidepods as inverted wings and seal the edges: the car makes downforce without making drag
cars.innovations: Ground effect, and sliding skirts to seal the low-pressure area at the car's edges
cars.story: Wings make downforce and pay for it in drag. Peter Wright's insight was that the whole underbody could be a wing instead, and that the ground itself would double the effect if the sides were sealed. The 78 was quick everywhere and unbeatable in slow corners. It should have won the 1977 championship and did not, because the DFV kept failing.
cars.outcome: 7 wins and 9 poles across 1977 and early 1978, before the 79 replaced it.

cars.designers: John Barnard, Alan Jenkins, Steve Nichols
cars.power_note: 510 bhp at 11,000 rpm; a TAG-Porsche turbo V6 of about 700 bhp was fitted late in 1983
cars.concept: Aluminium is not stiff enough to carry ground-effect loads; build the tub out of carbon fibre instead
cars.innovations: The first carbon-fibre composite monocoque to race in Formula One
cars.story: Barnard got the idea from Rolls-Royce engineers using carbon fibre in turbofan blades, and had the tub built by Hercules Aerospace in Utah because nobody in motor racing could make one. The paddock thought it would shatter. Then John Watson crashed heavily at Monza in 1981, the car broke apart around a tub that stayed intact, and he walked away. Every car on the grid was carbon-fibre within a few years, and it is the single largest reason drivers stopped dying.
cars.outcome: 43 races, 6 wins. No championships - its importance is structural, not competitive.

cars.designers: Aurelio Lampredi
cars.power_note: The 2.0-litre Formula Two engine; the related 625 F1 car took the same design out to 2,498 cc and 210-230 hp
cars.suspension: Front: independent, transverse leaf springs with Houdaille dampers. Rear: de Dion axle
cars.concept: A Formula Two car that won two World Championships because the championship came to it
cars.story: When Alfa withdrew after 1951 there were not enough Formula One cars left to fill a grid, so the 1952 and 1953 championships were run to Formula Two rules. Ferrari already had the best Formula Two car. Ascari won every championship race he entered in 1952 bar the Indianapolis 500, and all but the last in 1953: seven straight wins, a record that stood for sixty years until Vettel beat it in 2013.
cars.outcome: Ascari's back-to-back titles, 1952 and 1953.

cars.designers: Derek Gardner
cars.suspension: Double wishbone front and rear, coil springs over dampers, anti-roll bars
cars.concept: Four small front wheels hide inside the body: less frontal area, more braking and cornering rubber
cars.innovations: Six wheels, with four 10-inch front tyres
cars.story: It worked. Scheckter and Depailler finished first and second at Anderstorp in 1976 and Tyrrell was third in the championship. It stopped working because Goodyear had no reason to keep developing a tyre size only one team used, so the front tyres fell behind while everyone else's improved. The 1977 car was heavier and slower, the idea was dropped, and the rules were later changed to require exactly four wheels.
cars.outcome: 30 races, 1 win, 1 pole, 14 podiums - the only six-wheeled car ever to win a World Championship race.

cars.designers: Andre de Cortanze, Jean-Pierre Jabouille, Francois Castaing
cars.power_note: About 510 bhp at 11,000 rpm; a single turbo at first, twin turbos later to attack the lag
cars.concept: The rules allow 1.5 litres with a turbocharger against 3.0 without; nobody has tried it, so try it
cars.innovations: The first turbocharged engine in Formula One, and the first radial tyres
cars.story: It was slow, it was unreliable, and rival teams called it the yellow teapot for the cloud of white smoke it produced when it let go, which was often. It never won. But by 1983 every serious car had a turbo, by 1986 there was nothing else on the grid, and the naturally aspirated 3.0-litre engine that had defined Formula One since 1966 was gone.
cars.outcome: 25 races, no wins, one pole. The RS10 that followed it won at Dijon in 1979 - the first turbo victory.

cars.designers: Colin Chapman, Tony Rudd, Tony Southgate, Peter Wright, Martin Ogilvie, Geoff Aldridge
cars.power_note: 475 bhp at 11,000 rpm
cars.chassis_type: aluminium monocoque, strengthened for ground-effect loads
cars.suspension: Front: double wishbone, inboard spring/damper. Rear: parallel top links, lower wishbones, twin radius arms, outboard spring/damper
cars.concept: The 78 idea done properly: everything moved out of the airflow under the car so the tunnels run clean from front to back
cars.innovations: Full ground effect, with the fuel moved to a single central cell and the rear suspension repackaged to clear the diffuser exits
cars.story: The 78 proved the principle; the 79 removed everything that got in its way. Andretti said it was like being painted to the road. It was so far ahead that Chapman had already moved on to the 80, which failed, and then to the twin-chassis 88, which was banned - Lotus never won another championship. Every team copied the 79 for 1979, and Williams and Ligier did it better.
cars.outcome: 26 races, 6 wins, 10 poles. Andretti's 1978 title and Lotus's seventh and last constructors' championship.

cars.designers: Gordon Murray
cars.power_note: 520 bhp at 12,000 rpm
cars.suspension: Pullrod double wishbones front and rear
cars.concept: If a flat-12 is too wide for ground-effect tunnels, make the downforce a different way: extract the air from under the car with a fan
cars.innovations: Surface heat exchangers in place of radiators on the original BT46 (which did not work); on the BT46B, an engine-driven fan drawing air from a skirted underbody
cars.story: The fan was declared to be for cooling, which was true for about 30 per cent of what it did. Lauda won the 1978 Swedish Grand Prix by half a minute and the car was never raced again: Ecclestone owned Brabham and was building his position in FOCA, and the other team principals made withdrawing it the price. It remains the only car to win every Grand Prix it entered.
cars.outcome: The BT46B won the one race it started. The conventional BT46 won at Monza the same year.

cars.designers: Colin Chapman, Peter Wright, Tony Rudd, Martin Ogilvie
cars.suspension: Top rocker arms, lower wishbones, inboard springs front and rear
cars.concept: Two chassis, one inside the other: the outer one takes the aerodynamic load and runs stiff, the inner one carries the driver and rides softly
cars.innovations: The twin-chassis principle, and one of the first extensive uses of carbon fibre in a chassis
cars.story: Ground-effect cars had to run rock-hard suspension to keep the skirts sealed, which by 1981 was punishing enough to hurt drivers. Chapman's answer separated the two jobs. Rival teams protested that the sprung outer body was a movable aerodynamic device; the car was excluded from three race weekends and never started a Grand Prix. It is the clearest case in the sport's history of a rule stopping a genuinely good idea, and Chapman's disgust at it is usually read as the beginning of the end of Lotus.
cars.outcome: Never raced. Ran in practice at Long Beach, Rio and Silverstone in 1981 and was excluded each time.
