regulation_limits.note: The first wheelbase cap in the modern rules. A 2026 car quoted at 3,400 mm is being quoted the rule.
Widened from 1,800 mm for 2017; reduced again for 2026, which is what bounds this row.
Part of the 2026 reduction in car size.
The first minimum weight in Formula One; there was none before 1961.
Raised alongside mandatory bladder fuel cells.
Raised alongside safety foam in the fuel tanks.

Raised with the mandatory crushable structure around the fuel tanks. The 1980 regulations restate it unchanged, which is what bounds this row rather than an assumption that nothing happened in between.
Raised with the survival cell extending to the driver's feet.
Reduced when rigid skirts were legalised.
Reduced when ground-effect undertrays were outlawed.
Reduced when naturally aspirated engines were re-allowed at 3,500 cc.
Raised with the mandatory static crash test. The next change this source records is 2004, so the row stops here rather than carry a 1988 figure through the 1990s.
605 kg in qualifying, and not below 600 kg at any other time, including driver and fuel.
The last year of the V8 formula. The hybrid rules raised it again for 2014; this source does not give that figure, so the row stops here.
Raised with the wider car and wider tyres.
Recorded only because the 2025 change is stated as an increase FROM 798 kg, which fixes the 2024 figure.
Raised by 2 kg for the higher driver allowance and 5 kg for the mandated driver cooling system.

The first deliberate weight reduction in decades: 722 kg of car and driver plus 46 kg of estimated tyre mass in the FIA overview. Every 2026 car will be built to this number, so it says nothing about any one of them.

circuits.name: Autodromo Oscar Galvez
circuits.characteristics: A municipal autodrome with several selectable configurations
circuits.notes: Hosted the Argentine GP in three spells; the 1953 race saw spectators killed when a car left the road into an unprotected crowd.

circuits.name: Adelaide Street Circuit
circuits.characteristics: Fast street circuit with a long straight along Dequetteville Terrace
circuits.notes: Hosted the season finale for eleven years, deciding the 1986, 1990 and 1994 championships.

circuits.name: Albert Park
circuits.characteristics: Parkland roads around a lake; smooth, low-grip early in the weekend, fast flowing middle sector
circuits.notes: Australia's championship rounds ran at Adelaide 1985-1995 before moving to Melbourne. Reprofiled in 2021: the chicane at Turns 9-10 removed and several corners widened, cutting lap times by around five seconds.

circuits.name: Red Bull Ring
circuits.characteristics: Only ten corners and the shortest lap time of the season; steep gradients and three long uphill straights
circuits.notes: Originally the 5.9 km Osterreichring (1970-1987), shortened as the A1-Ring (1997-2003), then rebuilt by Red Bull and returned in 2014. Track-limits penalties at Turns 9 and 10 have become a recurring controversy.

circuits.name: Zeltweg Airfield
circuits.characteristics: A bumpy square laid out on concrete airfield runways
circuits.notes: One Grand Prix, in 1964; the surface destroyed suspensions and the race moved to the Osterreichring.

circuits.name: Baku City Circuit
circuits.characteristics: A 2.2 km flat-out run to Turn 1 combined with a castle section barely eight metres wide
circuits.notes: Held as the European GP in 2016 before becoming the Azerbaijan GP. Consistently produces chaotic races because of the combination of high top speed and zero margin for error.

circuits.name: Bahrain International Circuit
circuits.characteristics: Desert circuit with three heavy braking zones; abrasive surface and a large day-to-night temperature swing
circuits.notes: The first Grand Prix in the Middle East. Long the venue for pre-season testing. The 2020 Sakhir GP used the short 'outer' loop, producing a lap time of 53 seconds.

circuits.name: Circuit Zolder
circuits.characteristics: A stand-in for Spa during the years the old circuit was considered too dangerous
circuits.notes: Gilles Villeneuve was killed here in qualifying on 8 May 1982.

circuits.name: Circuit de Spa-Francorchamps
circuits.characteristics: The longest lap of the season, 100 m of elevation change, and Eau Rouge-Raidillon taken flat in modern cars
circuits.notes: The original 14.1 km road circuit ran until 1970 and was dropped as too dangerous. The shortened layout returned in 1983. Anthoine Hubert was killed here in an F2 race in 2019 at Raidillon, which was subsequently reprofiled with greater run-off.

circuits.name: Nivelles-Baulers
circuits.characteristics: Flat and featureless, with vast run-off
circuits.notes: One of the alternatives used while Spa was off the calendar.

circuits.name: Autodromo Jose Carlos Pace (Interlagos)
circuits.characteristics: Anti-clockwise, undulating and short; the Senna S and the long uphill run to the line make it a strong overtaking circuit
circuits.notes: Named after the Brazilian driver Jose Carlos Pace. Shortened from 7.96 km in 1990. Has hosted an unusual number of title deciders, including 2008 and 2021.

circuits.name: Jacarepagua
circuits.characteristics: Flat, hot and abrasive; a long pit straight and a longer back straight with grandstands giving a view of the whole lap
circuits.notes: Opened in 1978 and originally called the Autodromo Internacional do Rio de Janeiro; renamed for Nelson Piquet in 1988 after his third title. Hosted the Brazilian Grand Prix in 1978 and from 1981 to 1989, after which the race returned permanently to Interlagos. Demolished in 2012 for the 2016 Olympic park.

circuits.name: Circuit Gilles-Villeneuve
circuits.characteristics: Semi-permanent island circuit; heavy braking, low grip, and the Wall of Champions at the final chicane
circuits.notes: Named after Gilles Villeneuve, who won the inaugural race here in 1978. The Wall of Champions earned its name in 1999 when Hill, Villeneuve Jr and Schumacher all hit it.

circuits.name: Circuit Mont-Tremblant
circuits.characteristics: Extremely undulating; drivers complained of bruising from the bumps
circuits.notes: Hosted two Grands Prix before being dropped on safety grounds.

circuits.name: Mosport Park
circuits.characteristics: Fast, hilly and increasingly considered unsafe by the mid-1970s
circuits.notes: Alternated the Canadian GP with Mont-Tremblant.

circuits.name: Shanghai International Circuit
circuits.characteristics: Tightening 270-degree opening complex, then the longest back straight of the season into a heavy braking zone
circuits.notes: Designed by Hermann Tilke on marshland, requiring tens of thousands of concrete piles. The layout traces the Chinese character 'shang'. Absent from the calendar 2020-2023.

circuits.name: Bugatti Circuit
circuits.characteristics: The short permanent circuit at Le Mans, using the pit straight of the 24-hour course
circuits.notes: One Grand Prix, in 1967, poorly attended and never repeated.

circuits.name: Charade
circuits.characteristics: Laid out around an extinct volcano; nicknamed the French Nurburgring
circuits.notes: Dropped after loose volcanic stone caused injuries, including the eye injury that ended Helmut Marko's career in 1972.

circuits.name: Circuit Paul Ricard
circuits.characteristics: The blue-and-red striped Blue Zone run-off, abrasive by design, in place of gravel traps
circuits.notes: Hosted the French GP in two spells. The Mistral straight was split by a chicane for the modern configuration.

circuits.name: Circuit de Nevers Magny-Cours
circuits.characteristics: Famously smooth surface; the Adelaide hairpin was the main overtaking point
circuits.notes: Hosted the French GP after Paul Ricard, in a location chosen for regional development rather than accessibility.

circuits.name: Dijon-Prenois
circuits.characteristics: Short and hilly, with a lap so brief that the field spread quickly
circuits.notes: Site of the 1979 Villeneuve-Arnoux duel over the final two laps.

circuits.name: Reims-Gueux
circuits.characteristics: Public-road triangle where slipstreaming decided races
circuits.notes: The 1961 French GP finish was decided by 0.1 s after a race-long slipstreaming battle.

circuits.name: Rouen-les-Essarts
circuits.characteristics: Downhill cobbled hairpin section through a forest
circuits.notes: Jo Schlesser was killed here in 1968 in the magnesium-bodied Honda RA302.

circuits.name: AVUS
circuits.characteristics: Two long parallel straights joined by a 43-degree banked brick wall turn
circuits.notes: One Grand Prix, in 1959, run in two heats. Jean Behra was killed in a supporting sports-car race.

circuits.name: Hockenheimring
circuits.characteristics: Since 2002 a short stadium-based lap; before that, 6.8 km of flat-out running through the forest
circuits.notes: Jim Clark was killed here in a Formula 2 race in 1968. The forest section was abandoned in 2002 on cost and safety grounds, to considerable regret.

circuits.name: Nurburgring (GP-Strecke)
circuits.characteristics: A modern circuit built alongside the Nordschleife; technical and often cold and wet
circuits.notes: Hosted the European, Luxembourg and German Grands Prix at various times.

circuits.name: Nurburgring Nordschleife
circuits.characteristics: The Green Hell: 22.8 km, more than 170 corners and 300 m of elevation change
circuits.notes: Stewart's 1968 win in fog and rain by four minutes, and Fangio's 1957 charge, are among the sport's defining drives. Dropped after Lauda's near-fatal crash in 1976 — the circuit was impossible to marshal or make safe.

circuits.name: Nurburgring Sudschleife
circuits.characteristics: The southern loop of the Nurburgring complex
circuits.notes: Never used for a World Championship round. Held in the register because the 1960 German Grand Prix ran here: that race was run to Formula Two regulations after safety concerns at AVUS and did not count towards the championship, so it is absent from the race table.

circuits.name: Hungaroring
circuits.characteristics: Tight, twisty and dusty; often described as Monaco without the walls. Track position is everything
circuits.notes: The first Grand Prix held behind the Iron Curtain, and a landmark in the sport's commercial expansion. Has been on every calendar since 1986.

circuits.name: Buddh International Circuit
circuits.characteristics: Fast and undulating, with a double-apex Turn 10-11 taken at high speed
circuits.notes: Dropped after three races over a tax dispute with Indian authorities.

circuits.name: Autodromo Enzo e Dino Ferrari
circuits.official_name: Autodromo Internazionale Enzo e Dino Ferrari
circuits.characteristics: Old-school, narrow, anti-clockwise and almost impossible to overtake on in modern cars
circuits.notes: Hosted the San Marino GP 1981-2006 and the Italian GP in 1980. Ayrton Senna and Roland Ratzenberger were killed here in the weekend of 30 April-1 May 1994; the circuit was heavily modified afterwards, with Tamburello and Villeneuve turned into chicanes. Returned in 2020.

circuits.name: Autodromo Nazionale Monza
circuits.characteristics: The Temple of Speed: lowest downforce configuration of the year and the highest average speed
circuits.notes: Built in 1922, the third purpose-built permanent motor circuit in the world. Has held every Italian GP but one (Imola, 1980). The banked oval was used in combination with the road course in 1955-56 and 1960-61.

circuits.name: Mugello Circuit
circuits.characteristics: Fast, flowing and hilly; among the most highly rated circuits by drivers
circuits.notes: Ferrari-owned. Hosted a single Grand Prix, the 2020 Tuscan GP, which marked Ferrari's 1,000th championship start.

circuits.name: Pescara
circuits.characteristics: The longest circuit ever to hold a World Championship Grand Prix
circuits.notes: A single race in 1957, added late in the year when financial difficulties cancelled other rounds.

circuits.name: Fuji Speedway
circuits.characteristics: One of the longest straights in the sport, running downhill from the base of Mount Fuji
circuits.notes: Hosted Japan's first two Grands Prix in 1976-77, including the 1976 title decider in torrential rain, then returned in 2007-08.

circuits.name: Suzuka Circuit
circuits.characteristics: The only figure-of-eight in the championship; the Esses and 130R reward commitment above all
circuits.notes: Built by Honda in 1962 as a test track, designed by Dutchman John Hugenholtz. Has decided more championships than any other venue. Jules Bianchi was fatally injured here in 2014.

circuits.name: TI Circuit Aida
circuits.characteristics: Short, narrow and tight
circuits.notes: Hosted the Pacific Grand Prix in 1994 and 1995 so Japan could stage two races.

circuits.name: Sepang International Circuit
circuits.characteristics: Two enormously wide straights joined by a hairpin, extreme heat and reliable afternoon thunderstorms
circuits.notes: Tilke's first F1 commission and the template for the modern purpose-built venue. Held the Malaysian GP 1999-2017; returns to the calendar in 2026 as the host of the Bahrain Grand Prix while Sakhir is rebuilt.

circuits.name: Autodromo Hermanos Rodriguez
circuits.characteristics: 2,285 m above sea level — thin air means minimum drag, maximum cooling difficulty and unusual power-unit behaviour
circuits.notes: Named for Ricardo and Pedro Rodriguez, both killed racing. Ran 1963-1970 and 1986-1992 before returning in 2015 with the final sector routed through the Foro Sol baseball stadium.

circuits.name: Circuit de Monaco
circuits.characteristics: The slowest, narrowest and most unforgiving circuit in the championship; qualifying is decisive
circuits.notes: Run since 1929 and part of the championship from its first season, missing only 1951-54 and 2020. Senna won here six times, five of them consecutively. Overtaking is so difficult that a two-stop rule was introduced in 2025 to force strategic variation.

circuits.name: Ain-Diab
circuits.characteristics: Coastal public roads
circuits.notes: Hosted the 1958 title decider. Stuart Lewis-Evans suffered fatal burns in the race, prompting Vanwall's withdrawal from the sport.

circuits.name: Circuit Zandvoort
circuits.characteristics: Dune circuit with two banked corners — Hugenholtz (18 degrees) and the final Arie Luyendyk bend
circuits.notes: Ran 1952-1985, then returned in 2021 on the back of Verstappen's popularity. Banking was added to the final corner to help cars follow through it onto the main straight.

circuits.name: Autodromo Internacional do Algarve
circuits.characteristics: Severe elevation change and several blind crests; a rollercoaster of a lap
circuits.notes: Added to the calendar during the COVID-affected seasons.

circuits.name: Autodromo do Estoril
circuits.characteristics: A long, banked final corner onto an extended main straight
circuits.notes: Senna's first Grand Prix win came here in the rain in 1985, in a Lotus.

circuits.name: Boavista
circuits.characteristics: Cobbled city streets with tram lines
circuits.notes: Alternated the Portuguese GP with Monsanto.

circuits.name: Monsanto Park
circuits.characteristics: Parkland circuit above Lisbon
circuits.notes: One Grand Prix, in 1959.

circuits.name: Lusail International Circuit
circuits.characteristics: A motorcycle circuit adapted for F1: fast, flowing medium-speed corners that load the tyres continuously
circuits.notes: The sustained lateral loads caused tyre sidewall failures in 2023, forcing a mandatory stint-length limit.

circuits.name: Sochi Autodrom
circuits.characteristics: Laid out through the Winter Olympic park; a long, flat, low-degradation lap dominated by one 90-degree corner
circuits.notes: The Russian GP was cancelled in 2022 and the contract terminated following the invasion of Ukraine.

circuits.name: Jeddah Corniche Circuit
circuits.characteristics: The fastest street circuit ever built, averaging over 250 km/h with blind walled kinks
circuits.notes: Its sight lines and lack of run-off have drawn sustained criticism from drivers.

circuits.name: Marina Bay Street Circuit
circuits.characteristics: The first night race; bumpy, humid, high-downforce and physically the most demanding event of the year
circuits.notes: Drivers lose two to three kilograms in a race here. The 2008 inaugural event was later found to have been decided by a deliberately crashed Renault — the 'Crashgate' affair. Shortened and reprofiled in 2023.

circuits.name: Kyalami
circuits.characteristics: High altitude and a long uphill main straight
circuits.notes: Hosted the South African GP in two configurations. Not used since 1993; periodically discussed as a candidate for a return.

circuits.name: Prince George Circuit
circuits.characteristics: Coastal road circuit
circuits.notes: Hosted the South African GP before Kyalami took over.

circuits.name: Korea International Circuit
circuits.characteristics: A permanent opening section and a street-style second half through a marina development that was never built
circuits.notes: Completed so late that FIA homologation arrived days before the first race.

circuits.name: Circuit de Barcelona-Catalunya
circuits.characteristics: A test-track archetype: fast opening sector rewarding aerodynamic load, slow final sector rewarding traction
circuits.notes: The sport's default winter testing venue for two decades, which makes it the circuit teams understand best and the one that most reliably ranks cars by raw performance. The Turn 10 chicane added in 2007 was removed in 2023.

circuits.name: Circuito de Jerez
circuits.characteristics: Technical and hard on the front tyres
circuits.notes: Site of the closest finish in F1 history — 0.014 s between Mansell and Senna in 1986 — and of Schumacher's 1997 collision with Villeneuve.

circuits.name: Circuito del Jarama
circuits.characteristics: Narrow and twisty; the 1981 race finished with five cars covered by 1.24 seconds
circuits.notes: Designed by John Hugenholtz.

circuits.name: Madrid IFEMA
circuits.characteristics: New for 2026: a mix of public roads and permanent sections around the IFEMA exhibition centre, including a banked turn
circuits.notes: Spain's second race on the 2026 calendar. Contracted to become the sole Spanish round from 2027, when Barcelona's deal ends.

circuits.name: Montjuic
circuits.characteristics: Fast, dangerous parkland street circuit on a hill above Barcelona
circuits.notes: The 1975 race was stopped after 29 laps when Rolf Stommelen's car went over a barrier and killed four bystanders. Lella Lombardi's half-point for sixth remains the only World Championship score by a woman.

circuits.name: Pedralbes
circuits.characteristics: Wide boulevards in the Barcelona suburbs
circuits.notes: Abandoned after the 1955 Le Mans disaster prompted a reassessment of street racing.

circuits.name: Valencia Street Circuit
circuits.characteristics: Harbour-side street circuit with a swing bridge; almost no overtaking
circuits.notes: Hosted the European GP. Widely considered one of the least successful venues of the modern era.

circuits.name: Scandinavian Raceway
circuits.characteristics: Built on a marsh with an airstrip forming the main straight
circuits.notes: The Swedish GP existed because of Ronnie Peterson and Gunnar Nilsson; it ended when both were gone.

circuits.name: Bremgarten
circuits.characteristics: Fast, tree-lined roads through a forest with constantly changing light and no straights of note
circuits.notes: Switzerland banned circuit racing after the 1955 Le Mans disaster; the ban was only partially lifted in 2022 and no championship race has been held there since 1954.

circuits.name: Istanbul Park
circuits.characteristics: Turn 8: a quadruple-apex left-hander taken at over 260 km/h, one of the great modern corners
circuits.notes: Widely regarded as the best of the Tilke-designed circuits. Held the Turkish GP 2005-2011 and returned as a COVID-era replacement in 2020-21.

circuits.name: Yas Marina Circuit
circuits.characteristics: Day-into-night race; reprofiled in 2021 to remove the slow hairpin section and open up the corners
circuits.notes: Has hosted the season finale in all but one of its years. The 2021 finish here — a safety-car restart applied contrary to the regulations — led to the removal of the race director and a restructuring of race control.

circuits.name: Aintree
circuits.characteristics: Flat circuit laid out around the Grand National horse-racing course
circuits.notes: Stirling Moss's 1955 win here was the first by a British driver in a British Grand Prix.

circuits.name: Brands Hatch
circuits.characteristics: Natural amphitheatre; Paddock Hill Bend drops sharply away on the exit
circuits.notes: Alternated the British GP with Silverstone from 1964 to 1986 and also held the European and Race of Champions events.

circuits.name: Donington Park
circuits.characteristics: Undulating parkland circuit with the fast Craner Curves
circuits.notes: Hosted one Grand Prix, the 1993 European GP, in which Senna passed four cars on the opening lap in the wet — one of the most celebrated laps in the sport.

circuits.name: Silverstone Circuit
circuits.characteristics: High-speed and high-energy: Copse, Maggotts-Becketts-Chapel and Stowe are among the fastest corner sequences in the sport
circuits.notes: Hosted the first ever World Championship Grand Prix on 13 May 1950, on a wartime bomber airfield. The British GP alternated with Aintree and Brands Hatch before settling here permanently in 1987.

circuits.name: Caesars Palace
circuits.characteristics: A flat, featureless layout in a hotel car park
circuits.notes: Decided the 1981 and 1982 championships despite being widely disliked.

circuits.name: Circuit of The Americas
circuits.characteristics: A deliberate anthology circuit: a blind uphill Turn 1, a Silverstone-style Esses, and a Hockenheim-style stadium section
circuits.notes: The first purpose-built F1 venue in the United States. Notorious for a bumpy surface caused by ground subsidence.

circuits.name: Detroit Street Circuit
circuits.characteristics: Bumpy concrete-walled streets around the Renaissance Center
circuits.notes: One of four US venues used in the 1980s alongside Long Beach, Las Vegas and Dallas.

circuits.name: Fair Park
circuits.characteristics: Temporary circuit whose surface broke up in 40 C heat during the race
circuits.notes: A single Grand Prix in 1984; Mansell collapsed pushing his car to the line.

circuits.name: Indianapolis Motor Speedway
circuits.characteristics: The championship used the 2.5-mile oval 1950-60 and an infield road course running the opposite way round 2000-2007
circuits.notes: The Indianapolis 500 counted towards the World Championship from 1950 to 1960 although F1 regulars almost never entered. The 2005 US GP was contested by six cars after Michelin declared its tyres unsafe for the banking — a reputational disaster for the sport in America.

circuits.name: Las Vegas Strip Circuit
circuits.characteristics: Long, cold, low-grip night race down the Strip with speeds over 340 km/h
circuits.notes: The sport's third attempt at Las Vegas, after the Caesars Palace car park races of 1981-82. Promoted directly by Formula 1 itself rather than a local promoter.

circuits.name: Long Beach
circuits.characteristics: Harbour-side street circuit with a long Shoreline Drive straight
circuits.notes: The 'Monaco of America'; switched to IndyCar after 1983 and still runs today.

circuits.name: Miami International Autodrome
circuits.characteristics: Temporary roads around the Hard Rock Stadium; two long straights and a slow, bumpy technical section under the freeway
circuits.notes: One of three US races on the calendar since 2023 — the most for any country since the sport's early years.

circuits.name: Phoenix Street Circuit
circuits.characteristics: Downtown grid streets in extreme heat
circuits.notes: Attendance in 1991 was reportedly beaten by a local ostrich race, and the US GP then disappeared from the calendar for nine years.

circuits.name: Riverside
circuits.characteristics: Fast desert road course with a long back straight
circuits.notes: One Grand Prix, in 1960, won by Stirling Moss.

circuits.name: Sebring
circuits.characteristics: Former airfield, notoriously bumpy where concrete meets tarmac
circuits.notes: Hosted the first United States Grand Prix in 1959, where Bruce McLaren became the youngest winner to that date.

circuits.name: Watkins Glen
circuits.characteristics: Fast, sweeping and hilly, with a notoriously rough surface in later years
circuits.notes: Hosted the United States GP for twenty consecutive years. Dropped after 1980 on safety and financial grounds.

Chicane added before the Peraltada; the layout of Mansell's 1990 pass around the outside of Berger
Returned with the final sector routed slowly through the Foro Sol baseball stadium
The original wartime airfield perimeter road
Start line moved from Farm to the Woodcote straight
Chicane inserted at Woodcote after the 1973 first-lap pile-up
Second chicane added at Bridge as speeds rose again
Wholesale redesign: the Becketts complex, Vale and Priory replace the flat-out perimeter
Copse tightened and an Abbey chicane added in the 1994 safety review
Abbey chicane reprofiled
Abbey rebuilt as a left-right chicane; the layout of the Schumacher-Hakkinen era
New infield loop between Abbey and Brooklands; the pit complex moved to the Wellington Straight for 2011
Public roads through the Ardennes; abandoned as unmarshallable at modern speeds
Shortened permanent circuit retaining Eau Rouge and Blanchimont
Twenty-one corners, widely criticised for producing processional races
Hairpin, banked curve and faster final sector to improve overtaking, in place for the 2021 title decider

grands_prix.name: British Grand Prix
grands_prix.notes: Held every season since 1950 - one of only two events with an unbroken run.

grands_prix.name: Italian Grand Prix
grands_prix.circuits_used: Autodromo Nazionale Monza,Autodromo Enzo e Dino Ferrari
grands_prix.notes: The other event held every season since 1950. All but one at Monza.

grands_prix.name: Monaco Grand Prix
grands_prix.notes: Part of the Triple Crown of motorsport. Missing only 1951-54 and 2020.

grands_prix.name: French Grand Prix
grands_prix.circuits_used: Reims-Gueux,Rouen-les-Essarts,Charade,Bugatti Circuit,Circuit Paul Ricard,Dijon-Prenois,Circuit de Nevers Magny-Cours
grands_prix.notes: The oldest Grand Prix of all, first run in 1906. Absent since 2022.

grands_prix.name: Swiss Grand Prix
grands_prix.notes: Ended with Switzerland's ban on circuit racing after the 1955 Le Mans disaster.

grands_prix.name: Indianapolis 500
grands_prix.notes: Counted towards the World Championship 1950-1960. Run to American national rules by largely American entrants; almost no Formula One regular took part.

grands_prix.name: Spanish Grand Prix
grands_prix.circuits_used: Pedralbes,Circuito del Jarama,Montjuic,Circuito de Jerez,Circuit de Barcelona-Catalunya

grands_prix.name: Dutch Grand Prix
grands_prix.notes: Ran 1952-1985; returned 2021.

grands_prix.name: Pescara Grand Prix
grands_prix.notes: A single running, in 1957, on the longest circuit ever used - 25.579 km.

grands_prix.name: Moroccan Grand Prix
grands_prix.notes: A single running, in 1958, which decided that year's championship.

grands_prix.name: Portuguese Grand Prix
grands_prix.circuits_used: Boavista,Monsanto Park,Autodromo do Estoril,Autodromo Internacional do Algarve

grands_prix.name: United States Grand Prix
grands_prix.circuits_used: Sebring,Riverside,Watkins Glen,Phoenix Street Circuit,Indianapolis Motor Speedway,Circuit of The Americas

grands_prix.name: Mexican Grand Prix
grands_prix.notes: Renamed the Mexico City Grand Prix from 2021.

grands_prix.name: Brazilian Grand Prix
grands_prix.notes: Renamed the Sao Paulo Grand Prix from 2021.

grands_prix.name: Swedish Grand Prix
grands_prix.notes: Existed because of Ronnie Peterson and Gunnar Nilsson; ended when both were gone.

grands_prix.name: United States Grand Prix West
grands_prix.notes: The Long Beach race, run alongside a separate United States Grand Prix.

grands_prix.name: Caesars Palace Grand Prix
grands_prix.notes: Two runnings in a Las Vegas hotel car park, both deciding the championship.

grands_prix.name: San Marino Grand Prix
grands_prix.notes: A second Italian race under a flag of convenience.

grands_prix.name: European Grand Prix
grands_prix.circuits_used: Brands Hatch,Nurburgring (GP-Strecke),Donington Park,Circuito de Jerez,Valencia Street Circuit,Baku City Circuit
grands_prix.notes: A movable title used to allow a second race in one country.

grands_prix.name: Dallas Grand Prix
grands_prix.notes: A single running, in 1984, on a surface that broke up in 40 C heat.

grands_prix.name: Hungarian Grand Prix
grands_prix.notes: The first Grand Prix held behind the Iron Curtain.

grands_prix.name: Pacific Grand Prix
grands_prix.notes: Run at TI Circuit Aida so Japan could stage two races.

grands_prix.name: Bahrain Grand Prix
grands_prix.notes: First Grand Prix in the Middle East. Hosted at Sepang in 2026.

grands_prix.name: Singapore Grand Prix
grands_prix.notes: The sport's first night race.

grands_prix.name: Russian Grand Prix
grands_prix.notes: Contract terminated after the invasion of Ukraine.

grands_prix.name: Emilia-Romagna Grand Prix
grands_prix.notes: Imola's return under a new name. Both spellings appear in the record; they are the same event.

grands_prix.name: Styrian Grand Prix
grands_prix.notes: A second Red Bull Ring race, in 2020 and 2021.

grands_prix.name: 70th Anniversary Grand Prix
grands_prix.notes: A second Silverstone race in 2020, marking 70 years of the championship.

grands_prix.name: Tuscan Grand Prix
grands_prix.notes: A single running, at Mugello in 2020, which was Ferrari's 1,000th championship start.

grands_prix.name: Eifel Grand Prix
grands_prix.notes: A single running, at the Nurburgring in 2020.

grands_prix.name: Sakhir Grand Prix
grands_prix.notes: A second Bahrain race in 2020, on the short outer circuit - a 53-second lap.

grands_prix.name: Madrid Grand Prix
grands_prix.notes: New for 2026.

eras.summary: Grand Prix racing resumed with pre-war machinery and pre-war attitudes to risk. Fangio won five titles in eight seasons.
eras.defining_features: Front engines, drum brakes, no seatbelts, treaded road-style tyres, races of 500 km

eras.summary: Cooper put the engine behind the driver and the entire grid followed within three years. British 'garagiste' teams displaced the Italian manufacturers.
eras.defining_features: Mid-engined layout, monocoque chassis, the 1.5 L formula, the first Constructors' Championship

eras.era_name: The DFV and the birth of aerodynamics
eras.summary: The Cosworth DFV made independent constructors competitive; wings and then ground effect turned the car into an aerodynamic device. Fatality rates were at their worst.
eras.defining_features: 3.0 L formula, wings, sponsorship liveries, the beginning of the safety movement

eras.summary: Two revolutions at once: underbody downforce and forced induction. Power outputs reached figures never approached since.
eras.defining_features: Venturi tunnels, sliding skirts, 1,400 bhp qualifying engines, carbon-fibre chassis

eras.era_name: The electronic era and its aftermath
eras.summary: Active suspension, traction control and semi-automatic gearboxes arrived and were then banned. The 1994 accidents redefined the sport's relationship with risk.
eras.defining_features: Driver aids and their prohibition, the post-Imola safety programme, refuelling

eras.era_name: Ferrari's dominance and the manufacturer boom
eras.summary: Schumacher and Ferrari won five consecutive titles; car makers poured in money.
eras.defining_features: Grooved tyres, tyre wars, V10 then V8 engines, unlimited testing, escalating budgets

eras.summary: Rule packages designed to cut downforce were repeatedly outwitted — double diffusers, F-ducts, blown floors.
eras.defining_features: KERS, DRS, exhaust-blown diffusers, the arrival of Pirelli's degradation tyres

eras.summary: The most complex power units ever raced, and the longest period of single-team dominance in the sport's history.
eras.defining_features: 1.6 L V6 turbo hybrids, 50%+ thermal efficiency, eight consecutive Mercedes constructors' titles

eras.era_name: Ground effect returns and the cost cap bites
eras.summary: New aerodynamics intended to allow close following, alongside a budget cap that began to compress the field. Red Bull's 2023 was the most dominant season on record; by 2025 the top three drivers finished within thirteen points.
eras.defining_features: Venturi tunnels, porpoising, 18-inch wheels, the $135-145 m cost cap, sprint weekends

eras.summary: A smaller, lighter car, an even power split between combustion and electrical energy, sustainable fuel, and two new manufacturers.
eras.dominant_teams: TBD — Mercedes leads the opening half of 2026
eras.defining_features: Active aerodynamics, Overtake Mode, no MGU-H, 100% sustainable fuel, twelve teams

regulation_changes.title: World Championship established
regulation_changes.detail: The FIA created a Drivers' World Championship over six European Grands Prix plus the Indianapolis 500.
regulation_changes.impact: Turned a loose calendar of national Grands Prix into a single competition.

regulation_changes.title: Points to the top five plus fastest lap
regulation_changes.detail: 8-6-4-3-2 with one point for fastest lap, shared if tied. Only a driver's best four results counted.
regulation_changes.impact: Dropped scores would remain in some form until 1990.

regulation_changes.title: Championship run to Formula 2
regulation_changes.detail: 2.0 L naturally aspirated, adopted for 1952-53 after Alfa Romeo's withdrawal left too few competitive F1 cars.
regulation_changes.impact: Ascari won every race he entered across the two years.

regulation_changes.title: 2.5 L naturally aspirated formula
regulation_changes.detail: New capacity limit; supercharging limited to 750 cc and effectively abandoned.
regulation_changes.impact: Drew Mercedes and Lancia into the championship.

regulation_changes.title: International Cup for F1 Manufacturers
regulation_changes.detail: The first Constructors' Championship, awarded to Vanwall.
regulation_changes.impact: Made the constructor, not just the driver, a championship competitor.

regulation_changes.title: Commercial fuel mandated
regulation_changes.detail: Avgas replaced exotic alcohol fuel blends; race distances cut from 500 km to 300 km.
regulation_changes.impact: Cut power and cost, and shortened races to roughly two hours.

regulation_changes.title: 1.5 L formula
regulation_changes.detail: Capacity halved and a minimum weight of 450 kg imposed.
regulation_changes.impact: Fiercely opposed by British teams, who were unprepared; Ferrari dominated 1961.

regulation_changes.title: 3.0 L formula
regulation_changes.detail: Capacity doubled, or 1.5 L with forced induction.
regulation_changes.impact: 'The return of power'; the Cosworth DFV followed in 1967.

regulation_changes.title: Commercial sponsorship permitted
regulation_changes.detail: The FIA allowed liveries other than national racing colours.
regulation_changes.impact: Gold Leaf Team Lotus appeared in red, white and gold. The sport's commercial model begins here.

regulation_changes.title: High wings banned mid-season
regulation_changes.detail: Following strut failures for both Lotus drivers at Barcelona, tall aerofoils on unsprung mountings were outlawed.
regulation_changes.impact: Aerodynamic devices were henceforth required to be fixed to the sprung mass and limited in height.

regulation_changes.title: Mandatory deformable structure and fuel bag tanks
regulation_changes.detail: Crushable structures around fuel cells and self-sealing bag tanks required.
regulation_changes.impact: Directly reduced fire deaths, the era's dominant killer.

regulation_changes.title: Airbox regulations and safety structures
regulation_changes.detail: Rollover bar dimensions specified; onboard fire extinguishers and electrical cut-off required.

regulation_changes.title: Deformable structures around the cockpit
regulation_changes.detail: Side crash structures mandated.

regulation_changes.title: Tall airboxes banned
regulation_changes.detail: Mid-season ban following the airbox height arms race.

regulation_changes.title: First turbocharged car
regulation_changes.detail: Renault exploited the long-dormant 1.5 L forced-induction option with the RS01.
regulation_changes.impact: Began an eleven-year turbo arms race.

regulation_changes.title: First Concorde Agreement
regulation_changes.detail: Settled the FISA-FOCA war over commercial rights and rule-making between the governing body, the teams and the commercial rights holder.
regulation_changes.impact: Established the tripartite governance model that still applies.

regulation_changes.title: Sliding skirts banned; 6 cm ride height minimum
regulation_changes.detail: Aimed at killing ground effect.
regulation_changes.impact: Circumvented by hydropneumatic suspension that lowered the car at speed.

regulation_changes.title: Flat bottoms mandated
regulation_changes.detail: Underbody had to be flat between the axles, ending Venturi tunnels.
regulation_changes.impact: Cornering speeds fell sharply; downforce moved back to wings.

regulation_changes.title: Refuelling banned; 220 litre fuel limit
regulation_changes.detail: Race fuel capped to restrain turbo power.
regulation_changes.impact: Turbo engines were detuned for races and unleashed in qualifying.

regulation_changes.title: Naturally aspirated engines outlawed
regulation_changes.detail: Turbo-only season, the sole one in the sport's history.

regulation_changes.title: 4.0 bar boost limit; naturally aspirated cars readmitted
regulation_changes.detail: 3.5 L atmospheric engines permitted alongside boost-limited turbos, with separate trophies.
regulation_changes.impact: Began the managed phase-out of turbos.

regulation_changes.title: 2.5 bar boost limit and 150 litre fuel limit
regulation_changes.detail: Final year of turbo eligibility.
regulation_changes.impact: McLaren-Honda still won 15 of 16 races.

regulation_changes.title: Turbocharging banned
regulation_changes.detail: 3.5 L naturally aspirated only.
regulation_changes.impact: Ended the highest-power era in the sport's history.

regulation_changes.title: Dropped scores abolished
regulation_changes.detail: All results counted towards the championship for the first time.
regulation_changes.impact: Simplified the championship and ended the era of gross-versus-net point totals.

regulation_changes.title: Emergency in-season rule changes
regulation_changes.detail: After Imola: plank under the floor, reduced airbox and diffuser, larger cockpit opening, restricted front wing endplates.
regulation_changes.impact: The most abrupt safety intervention in the sport's history.

regulation_changes.title: Refuelling reintroduced
regulation_changes.detail: Mid-race refuelling permitted from 1994.
regulation_changes.impact: Made race strategy a central competitive variable for sixteen years.

regulation_changes.title: Electronic driver aids banned
regulation_changes.detail: Active suspension, traction control, ABS, four-wheel steering and launch control outlawed.
regulation_changes.impact: Cars became markedly harder to drive; the enforcement difficulty led to traction control being legalised again in 2001.

regulation_changes.title: 3.0 L capacity limit
regulation_changes.detail: Engine capacity cut from 3.5 L.
regulation_changes.impact: A direct response to the 1994 accidents.

regulation_changes.title: Higher cockpit sides mandated
regulation_changes.detail: Head protection raised around the cockpit rim.

regulation_changes.title: Narrow-track cars and grooved tyres
regulation_changes.detail: Track cut from 2.0 m to 1.8 m; three grooves front and four rear.
regulation_changes.impact: Cut cornering speed at the expense of mechanical grip.

regulation_changes.title: Traction control legalised
regulation_changes.detail: Reinstated from the Spanish GP because the ban had become unpoliceable.
regulation_changes.impact: Banned again in 2008 with the standard ECU.

regulation_changes.title: Points to the top eight; single-lap qualifying
regulation_changes.detail: 10-8-6-5-4-3-2-1 introduced; parc ferme rules restricted set-up changes after qualifying.
regulation_changes.impact: Deliberately designed to reduce Ferrari's margin.

regulation_changes.title: Team orders banned
regulation_changes.detail: Following the 2002 Austrian GP, orders that interfere with a race result were prohibited.
regulation_changes.impact: Repealed in 2011 as unenforceable.

regulation_changes.title: One engine per two race weekends; tyre changes banned
regulation_changes.detail: Engines had to last two events; tyres could not be changed during a race.
regulation_changes.impact: The tyre rule was abandoned after the 2005 US GP fiasco.

regulation_changes.title: 2.4 L V8 engines
regulation_changes.detail: V10s replaced to cut power and cost.

regulation_changes.title: Single tyre supplier
regulation_changes.detail: Bridgestone became the sole supplier after Michelin's withdrawal.
regulation_changes.impact: Ended tyre-war development and made tyres a controlled variable.

regulation_changes.title: Standard ECU
regulation_changes.detail: A single McLaren Electronic Systems ECU for all cars.
regulation_changes.impact: Made traction control and engine braking control enforceable to ban.

regulation_changes.title: Aerodynamic overhaul and KERS
regulation_changes.detail: Wide low front wing, narrow high rear wing, most bodywork appendages removed; optional 60 kW kinetic energy recovery.
regulation_changes.impact: First serious attempt to design for following another car. The double-diffuser loophole dominated the season.

regulation_changes.title: Refuelling banned; new points system
regulation_changes.detail: Race refuelling prohibited; 25-18-15-12-10-8-6-4-2-1 introduced with the field expanded to 24 cars.
regulation_changes.impact: Fuel loads at the start became a major performance factor.

regulation_changes.title: DRS and Pirelli high-degradation tyres
regulation_changes.detail: A driver-adjustable rear wing usable within one second of the car ahead in designated zones, and tyres designed to fall off deliberately.
regulation_changes.impact: Both were explicit attempts to manufacture overtaking; both remain contested on sporting-purity grounds.

regulation_changes.title: Double points at the finale
regulation_changes.detail: The last race awarded double points.
regulation_changes.impact: Used once, universally disliked, and dropped.

regulation_changes.title: 1.6 L V6 turbo-hybrid power units
regulation_changes.detail: ERS with MGU-K and MGU-H, 100 kg fuel limit and 100 kg/h flow limit; five power-unit elements per season.
regulation_changes.impact: The most radical technical change in the sport's history. Thermal efficiency passed 50%. Development costs pushed several independent engine builders out.

regulation_changes.title: Virtual Safety Car
regulation_changes.detail: A field-wide delta-time speed restriction introduced after Jules Bianchi's accident at Suzuka.
regulation_changes.impact: Allows yellow-flag conditions to be enforced without bunching the field.

regulation_changes.title: Wider cars and tyres
regulation_changes.detail: Cars widened to 2.0 m, wider tyres, larger diffuser and lower rear wing.
regulation_changes.impact: Lap records fell across the calendar; following became harder.

regulation_changes.title: Halo mandated
regulation_changes.detail: A titanium cockpit protection structure able to withstand 12 tonnes.
regulation_changes.impact: Initially unpopular on aesthetic grounds; credited with saving Leclerc at Spa 2018, Grosjean at Bahrain 2020 and Zhou at Silverstone 2022.

regulation_changes.title: Point for fastest lap
regulation_changes.detail: One point for the fastest lap, if finishing in the top ten.
regulation_changes.impact: Removed again from 2025.

regulation_changes.title: Cost cap introduced
regulation_changes.detail: A budget cap of $145 m for 2021, excluding driver salaries, marketing and the three highest-paid staff.
regulation_changes.impact: The most consequential governance change since the Concorde Agreement; designed to compress the competitive order.

regulation_changes.title: Sprint format trialled
regulation_changes.detail: Three events ran a short Saturday race setting the grid, with points to the top three.
regulation_changes.impact: Extended to six events; sprint results decoupled from the Grand Prix grid from 2024.

regulation_changes.title: Ground effect returns
regulation_changes.detail: Venturi tunnels reinstated with simplified over-body aerodynamics, 18-inch wheels and standardised parts.
regulation_changes.impact: Intended to let cars follow closely. Porpoising — aerodynamic bouncing — dominated the first season and forced a mid-2022 technical directive on floor stiffness and a vertical-oscillation metric.

regulation_changes.title: Floor edge and stiffness rules tightened
regulation_changes.detail: Floor edges raised and diffuser throat height increased to curb porpoising.

regulation_changes.title: Fastest lap point removed
regulation_changes.detail: The bonus point introduced in 2019 was dropped.
regulation_changes.impact: Removed an incentive for late 'free' pit stops by out-of-contention cars.

regulation_changes.title: Tougher homologation tests
regulation_changes.detail: Roll-hoop vertical impact requirement raised from 16 g to 20 g; a two-stage nose-cone concept introduced.

regulation_changes.title: Overtake Mode
regulation_changes.detail: A driver within one second at the detection point receives additional energy deployment — the FIA/F1 overview describes an extra 0.5 MJ and a raised deployment profile.
regulation_changes.impact: The successor mechanism to DRS's overtaking assistance.

regulation_changes.title: New chassis formula
regulation_changes.detail: Wheelbase capped at 3,400 mm, width reduced to 1,900 mm, minimum weight 768 kg (722 kg car and driver plus 46 kg estimated tyre mass in the FIA overview).
regulation_changes.impact: The first deliberate reduction in car size and weight in decades.

regulation_changes.title: Active aerodynamics replace DRS
regulation_changes.detail: Driver-operable front and rear wing systems with distinct low-drag and high-downforce modes.
regulation_changes.impact: Removes the DRS proximity mechanism in favour of a mode both cars can use.

regulation_changes.title: MGU-H removed
regulation_changes.detail: The turbo-driven heat-energy recovery unit is deleted from the power unit.
regulation_changes.impact: Cut cost and complexity; explicitly credited with attracting Audi, Ford and General Motors.

regulation_changes.title: Roughly 50/50 power split
regulation_changes.detail: Electrical output raised to approximately 350 kW, against a comparable figure from the internal combustion engine.

regulation_changes.title: 100% advanced sustainable fuel
regulation_changes.detail: Fully sustainable drop-in fuel mandated.
regulation_changes.impact: The sport's principal decarbonisation claim for the ruleset.

technical_innovations.description: Cooper's rear-engined 500 cc cars scaled up to Grand Prix racing by 1958-59.
technical_innovations.legacy: Universal from 1961; every F1 car since has had the engine behind the driver.

technical_innovations.description: Positively closed valves and direct fuel injection derived from aero-engine work.
technical_innovations.legacy: Injection became universal; desmodromics did not.

technical_innovations.description: A stressed-skin aluminium tub replacing the spaceframe.
technical_innovations.legacy: Halved chassis weight and roughly trebled torsional stiffness. Now universal, in carbon fibre.

technical_innovations.innovation: The Cosworth DFV as a stressed member
technical_innovations.description: The engine bolted directly to the rear of the monocoque and carried the suspension loads.
technical_innovations.legacy: Made the small independent constructor viable for two decades.

technical_innovations.description: Inverted aerofoils generating downforce.
technical_innovations.legacy: The single most important performance concept in the sport's history.

technical_innovations.description: Radiators moved from the nose to the flanks, giving a wedge profile and cleaner front-end airflow.
technical_innovations.legacy: Standard layout ever since.

technical_innovations.description: Four small front wheels to cut frontal area while retaining braking and grip.
technical_innovations.legacy: Won the 1976 Swedish GP. Tyre development killed it; four-wheel cars mandated from 1983.

technical_innovations.description: Inverted-wing underbody profiles with sliding skirts sealing the low-pressure area.
technical_innovations.legacy: Transformed cornering speed. Banned in 1983, reintroduced in modified form in 2022.

technical_innovations.description: 1.5 L forced-induction engine exploiting a long-ignored rule.
technical_innovations.legacy: Defined 1980s F1 and produced the highest power figures ever seen in the sport.

technical_innovations.description: A fan, nominally for cooling, extracting air from beneath the car to generate suction.
technical_innovations.legacy: Won its only race, the 1978 Swedish GP, and was withdrawn under pressure.

technical_innovations.description: The first F1 chassis made from carbon composite.
technical_innovations.legacy: Vastly stronger and lighter than aluminium; the foundation of modern survival-cell safety. Universal within four years.

technical_innovations.description: Electrohydraulic paddle-shift with no clutch pedal for upshifts.
technical_innovations.legacy: Universal by the mid-1990s.

technical_innovations.description: Computer-controlled hydraulic ride height maintaining optimum aerodynamic platform.
technical_innovations.legacy: Devastatingly effective; banned for 1994.

technical_innovations.description: A second brake pedal acting on one rear wheel to rotate the car.
technical_innovations.legacy: Banned once revealed, as a four-wheel-steering device.

technical_innovations.description: A sprung mass in the nose damping tyre oscillation and stabilising the aerodynamic platform.
technical_innovations.legacy: Banned mid-2006 as a movable aerodynamic device.

technical_innovations.description: Front wishbone mounting philosophies to clean up airflow under the nose.
technical_innovations.legacy: Superseded by pull-rod and high-nose concepts.

technical_innovations.description: A second-tier diffuser exploiting a gap in the wording of the 2009 rules.
technical_innovations.legacy: Effectively decided the 2009 championship; banned for 2011.

technical_innovations.description: 60 kW kinetic energy recovery under braking.
technical_innovations.legacy: The bridgehead to the hybrid era.

technical_innovations.description: A driver-operated duct stalling the rear wing on the straights for less drag.
technical_innovations.legacy: Banned for 2011 as a movable aerodynamic device operated by the driver.

technical_innovations.description: Exhaust gases routed into the diffuser to energise it, including off-throttle.
technical_innovations.legacy: Progressively restricted 2011-2013 through exhaust position rules.

technical_innovations.description: Driver-adjustable rear wing within one second of the car ahead.
technical_innovations.legacy: Replaced by active aerodynamics and Overtake Mode in 2026.

technical_innovations.description: Compressor at the front of the engine and turbine at the rear, joined by a shaft through the vee, with the MGU-H between them.
technical_innovations.legacy: Gave Mercedes a package advantage that took rivals several seasons to answer.

technical_innovations.description: A small pre-combustion chamber igniting an ultra-lean main charge.
technical_innovations.legacy: Took thermal efficiency past 50%, roughly double a typical road petrol engine.

technical_innovations.description: Elaborate flow-conditioning structures ahead of the sidepods.
technical_innovations.legacy: Largely legislated away for 2022 to reduce wake sensitivity.

technical_innovations.description: Pushing and pulling the steering column altered front wheel toe on the move.
technical_innovations.legacy: Legal in 2020, explicitly banned for 2021.

technical_innovations.description: A radical narrow-sidepod interpretation of the ground-effect rules.
technical_innovations.legacy: Abandoned after two seasons; a rare example of a distinctive concept that simply did not work.

safety_milestones.milestone: Fuel and crowd control questions raised
safety_milestones.trigger_event: Von Trips's Monza crash killing 15 spectators
safety_milestones.description: Spectator placement began to be treated as a design problem rather than a local matter.
Jackie Stewart's campaign for barriers, run-off, medical facilities and marshalling standards begins in earnest.

safety_milestones.trigger_event: Multiple fatalities including Clark, Spence, Schlesser and Bandini
safety_milestones.description: Rollover protection specified; full-face helmets adopted.

safety_milestones.milestone: Bag fuel tanks and deformable structures
safety_milestones.description: Self-sealing fuel cells became mandatory.
Standardised restraint and fire suppression.

safety_milestones.trigger_event: Roger Williamson's death in a fire at Zandvoort with no marshal intervention
safety_milestones.description: Marshalling and fire-crew standards overhauled alongside the car rules.

safety_milestones.milestone: Permanent medical car and travelling medical delegate
safety_milestones.description: Professor Sid Watkins appointed in 1978; a doctor now travels with the championship.

safety_milestones.milestone: Standardised race-start procedure and medical helicopter
safety_milestones.trigger_event: Ronnie Peterson's death after a delayed extraction at Monza
safety_milestones.description: A helicopter capable of flying must be on site or the race does not start.
Minimum crash structure ahead of the driver's feet.
Cars had to pass a static and then dynamic impact test to be eligible.

safety_milestones.milestone: Driver's feet behind the front axle line
safety_milestones.description: Ended the practice of pedals ahead of the front wheels.

safety_milestones.trigger_event: Deaths of Senna and Ratzenberger, injuries to Wendlinger, Barrichello and Lehto
safety_milestones.description: Immediate aerodynamic cuts, then a multi-year programme: higher cockpit sides, larger cockpit template, wheel tethers, stronger side impact structures, and the FIA Institute's crash-research programme.
Head and neck protection around the cockpit rim.
Tethers to retain wheels; strengthened repeatedly since, with double tethers from 2011.

safety_milestones.milestone: Higher cockpit sides and headrest energy absorption

safety_milestones.trigger_event: Basilar skull fractures in motorsport worldwide
safety_milestones.description: Head and neck support tethering the helmet to the shoulders; the single most effective driver-protection device of its generation.

safety_milestones.trigger_event: Felipe Massa struck by a loose spring at the Hungaroring; Henry Surtees killed in F2
safety_milestones.description: A ballistic strip added to helmet visors.

safety_milestones.milestone: Virtual Safety Car and closed pit-lane research
safety_milestones.description: VSC introduced for 2015; the accident also began the closed-cockpit research programme.
Recovery vehicles may not be on track without VSC or safety car.

safety_milestones.trigger_event: Bianchi's death and the Justin Wilson and Henry Surtees fatalities in other categories
safety_milestones.description: A titanium structure withstanding 12 tonnes, roughly the weight of a London bus. Credited with saving lives at Spa 2018, Bahrain 2020 and Silverstone 2022.

safety_milestones.milestone: Stronger chassis and higher-load survival cell
safety_milestones.description: Front and side impact loads increased substantially.
Preceded further increases after Zhou Guanyu's 2022 Silverstone crash, in which the roll hoop failed.

safety_milestones.trigger_event: Zhou Guanyu's inverted crash at Silverstone
safety_milestones.description: Roll-hoop homologation revised to eliminate pointed designs that could dig into the surface.

safety_milestones.milestone: Roll-hoop vertical test raised to 20 g
safety_milestones.description: Up from 16 g, alongside a two-stage nose-cone concept in the 2026 framework.

glossary.definition: The point at which a car is closest to the inside of a corner; the geometry of the apex determines corner entry and exit speed.
Vertical flow-conditioning surfaces between the front wheels and sidepods, largely legislated away for 2022.
Tyre surface failure caused by overheating from the inside out.
Shown to a driver about to be lapped, requiring them to let the faster car past.
Radio instruction to pit, from the German 'Boxenstopp'; used because it is easier to hear than 'pit'.
The front-to-rear distribution of braking force, adjustable from the cockpit.
A tight sequence of corners inserted to slow cars, usually retrofitted for safety.
Undisturbed airflow; a car in clean air produces full downforce, one following closely does not.
The commercial and governance contract between the FIA, the commercial rights holder and the teams. First signed 1981.
The annual spending limit on team operations, introduced in 2021 and excluding driver salaries, marketing and the three highest-paid staff.
Did Not Finish.
Drag Reduction System, 2011-2025: a driver-adjustable rear wing flap usable within one second of the car ahead in designated zones.
The loss of tyre performance over a stint, distinct from wear; Pirelli's tyres are specified to degrade deliberately.
A target lap time drivers must not beat, used to enforce Virtual Safety Car conditions.
The turbulent wake behind a car, which reduces the downforce of a car following closely.
Aerodynamically generated load pressing the car onto the track, increasing grip at the cost of drag.
Energy Recovery System: the electrical part of the power unit.
A locally worn patch on a tyre caused by locking a wheel under braking; produces vibration severe enough to force a pit stop.
The lap from the grid to the grid before the start, used to warm tyres and brakes.
Downforce generated by accelerating airflow under the car through Venturi tunnels. Used 1977-1982 and again from 2022.
Head and Neck Support device, mandatory since 2003, tethering the helmet to the shoulders to prevent basilar skull fracture.
The titanium cockpit protection structure mandated in 2018, able to withstand around 12 tonnes.
FIA certification that a car, part or circuit meets the regulations.
Lifting off the throttle before the braking point to save fuel, energy or brake temperature.
Motor Generator Unit - Heat, recovering energy from exhaust gases via the turbocharger. Used 2014-2025 and removed for 2026.
Motor Generator Unit - Kinetic, recovering energy under braking and deploying it as drive.
Discarded rubber off the racing line; drivers avoid it because it destroys grip.
Staying out longer than a rival, using clear air to build a gap before stopping.
The 2026 replacement for DRS: additional energy deployment for a car within one second at the detection point.
The state, from the start of qualifying, in which set-up changes are prohibited without a pit-lane start.
The lap range in which a stop makes strategic sense.
The wooden (Jabroc) skid block under the floor, introduced in 1994 to enforce a minimum ride height. Excessive wear means disqualification.
First place on the starting grid, awarded on qualifying time.
Violent vertical oscillation caused by ground-effect stall and recovery; the defining problem of the 2022 season.
The full hybrid assembly since 2014: internal combustion engine, turbocharger, MGU-K, energy store and control electronics (plus MGU-H until 2026).
The low-drag region behind a car, used to gain speed before an overtake.
A short Saturday race introduced in 2021, currently run at six events, with its own qualifying session since 2024.
The panel of four officials, including one former driver, who rule on incidents and apply penalties at each event.
The FIA licence required to race in F1, earned through a points system across junior categories. Introduced in its current form in 2016.
The British term for slipstream.
The white lines defining the circuit; a lap is deleted if all four wheels go beyond them.
Pitting before a rival and using fresh-tyre pace to emerge ahead when they stop.
A field-wide delta-time speed restriction introduced in 2015, allowing yellow-flag conditions without bunching the field.
Aerodynamic testing time allocated in inverse proportion to championship position, to compress the competitive order.

team_radio.speaker: Rob Smedley (race engineer) to Felipe Massa [pit-to-car]
team_radio.transcript: OK, so, Fernando is faster than you. Can you confirm you understood that message?
team_radio.context: Lap 48 at Hockenheim. Team orders were banned outright at the time. Massa slowed at Turn 6 on the next lap and let Alonso through to win. Ferrari were fined $100,000 and the result stood; the FIA gave up and repealed the ban on team orders for 2011.

team_radio.speaker: Christian Horner (team principal) to Sebastian Vettel [pit-to-car]
team_radio.transcript: This is silly, Seb. Come on.
team_radio.context: Lap 45 at Sepang. Red Bull had called 'Multi-Map 21' - a coded instruction for both drivers to turn the engines down and hold position, Webber first and Vettel second. Vettel passed him anyway and won. Webber's reply in the cool-down room afterwards, 'Multi 21, Seb. Yeah, Multi 21', is the line the incident is remembered by, but it was said face to face rather than over the radio.

team_radio.speaker: Fernando Alonso to McLaren [car-to-pit]
team_radio.context: Lap 27 at Suzuka, as Verstappen went past him on the straight. Alonso had left Ferrari for a McLaren-Honda that was down something like 150 bhp on the Mercedes; GP2 was the Formula One feeder series. Broadcast live, and it is the line that defined McLaren's Honda era.

team_radio.speaker: Michael Masi (race director) to Toto Wolff [race director to team]
team_radio.transcript: Toto, it's called a motor race, ok? We went car racing.
team_radio.context: The reply to Wolff, broadcast live on the world feed as the race ended.

team_radio.speaker: Toto Wolff (Mercedes) to race director Michael Masi [team to race director]
team_radio.context: Wolff's protest on the same channel moments later. Masi's reply - 'Toto, it's called a motor race, ok? We went car racing.' - was broadcast with it. Mercedes protested, lost, and did not appeal; the FIA's own review found the restart procedure had been misapplied, and Masi was removed from the role for 2022.

team_radio.speaker: Christian Horner (Red Bull) to race director Michael Masi [team to race director]
team_radio.transcript: these lapped cars out of the way
team_radio.context: The closing laps at Yas Marina, with the title live and a safety car out. Masi allowed only the cars between Hamilton and Verstappen to un-lap themselves, contrary to the usual procedure, and restarted for a single racing lap. Verstappen, on fresh tyres, passed Hamilton and took the championship.

known_gaps.description: race_entries in the DISTRIBUTED build holds the winner, the pole-sitter and the fastest-lap setter for every race - about 2.1 rows per race against a real field of 15 to 22. That is a licensing decision, not an unfinished harvest: the rows come from Jolpica-F1, whose Ergast data is CC BY-NC-SA - non-commercial, the most restrictive licence any source here carries - and this database is a function of what is in its own repository. Run tools/ergast_load.py locally and the gap closes on your copy: 25,995 rows across all 1,161 races, and the podium reconciliation passes at 7 of 7 exact. The driver register was the binding constraint until v2.13 and no longer is - it went from 244 to 862, and the rows skipped for an unresolvable driver from 5,490 to 33.
known_gaps.resolution: python3 tools/ergast_load.py --from-dump  (one hash-verified zip, a few seconds). Then rerun verify.py. What remains skipped is 33 rows for 14 drivers Jolpica records and F1DB does not hold at all, declared in data/results.py DRIVER_NON_MAPPING - a source disagreement, not a gap, and not something to close by inventing a driver.

known_gaps.area: the chassis each race was won in, where a season is ambiguous
known_gaps.description: The winning chassis is known for 874 of 1,161 races. It comes from F1DB's entry lists, resolved through the driver and the round: F1DB records which chassis a constructor ran in a SEASON and which driver an entrant ran in which ROUND, and the second is far sharper than the first. What is left is the entrants that ran more than one design and do not say which raced where - Gold Leaf Team Lotus in 1970 entered a 49C, a 72B and a 72C, so Rindt's wins stay NULL while Soler-Roig's single Garvey Team Lotus entry resolves. v_ambiguous_seasons lists them. The gap is concentrated before 1980 because a modern team runs one car all season while a 1960s constructor was a name several privateers entered several different chassis under.
known_gaps.resolution: Per-round chassis data, which no source in use here has. The season articles print a chassis column in the same results table the winners came from, and that column IS per round. Harvesting it is only safe with the check that now exists: a harvested chassis must appear in that constructor's entry list for that season, or be refused.

known_gaps.area: the car each pole was taken in, where the season is ambiguous
known_gaps.description: This was the largest gap in the car data and is now mostly closed. The pole and fastest-lap harvest recorded who set them but not what they drove, so 1,260 of 2,424 entries carried no constructor at all and could not reach a car. F1DB's per-round driver data supplies it: 99 per cent of entries now name a constructor, and NINE cars match their published career pole total exactly, where previously none could be checked for more than not exceeding it. What is left is the seasons a constructor ran more than one chassis, where attributing a pole to a particular car would be a guess - McLaren ran the M23 and the M26 through 1976 and 1977, and the blanket season claim gave the M23 sixteen poles against a published fourteen before this was checked.
known_gaps.resolution: Per-round chassis data, which no source in use here has. The remaining seasons are listed in v_ambiguous_seasons and in car_seasons where corroborated = 0.

known_gaps.area: lap times, tyre stints, pit stops, radio and telemetry
known_gaps.description: The laps, stints, pit_stops, race_control_messages and team_radio tables are EMPTY in the distributed database, and that is a licensing and reproducibility decision rather than a missing harvest. Two sources fill them, and between them they reach further back than the 2018 floor this gap used to describe. Jolpica's database dump has 628,454 race laps from 1996 and 12,627 pit stops from 2011 - twenty-two seasons more than was previously thought available - but its Ergast lineage is CC BY-NC-SA, non-commercial, so the rows are loaded locally and never committed. FastF1 reads the F1 live timing API, which begins in 2018 and for which nothing earlier exists in any retrievable form; it adds sectors, tyre compound, stints and race control, none of which Jolpica has. Both may hold the same race at once - the schema keys a lap on (race, source, driver, lap) precisely so they can be compared rather than one overwriting the other. Car telemetry (speed, throttle, brake, gear at about 4 Hz) is deliberately NOT stored here at all: it is hundreds of megabytes per weekend and fastf1_load.py writes it to Parquet beside the database.
known_gaps.resolution: python3 tools/ergast_load.py --from-dump --timing   (1996-, one hash-verified zip, about fifteen seconds), and/or pip install fastf1 && python3 tools/fastf1_load.py --years 2018-2026 --results --radio. Then ./f1 laps. verify.py re-derives each race's fastest lap from the lap times and checks it against the setter already stored from the pole harvest - 446 races, no disagreement.

known_gaps.area: pole, fastest lap and race times per race
known_gaps.description: The race_timing table is empty. These figures are published per race rather than per season, so filling them for 1950-2017 means reading 1,161 individual race articles, which was judged too expensive against what it returns. From 2018 the FastF1 loader supplies the same information at far greater resolution.
known_gaps.resolution: Either harvest race articles for the pre-2018 seasons, or accept that timing starts in 2018 and fill it with tools/fastf1_load.py.

known_gaps.area: circuit configuration as raced, for most circuits
known_gaps.description: Thirteen circuits have a complete configuration timeline: Spa, Monza, Silverstone, Hockenheim, Interlagos, Indianapolis, Catalunya, Albert Park, the Spielberg site, the Mexico City site, Bahrain, Marina Bay and Yas Marina. For every other circuit the database holds one set of figures - the most recent - so a 1976 Kyalami lap is reported at the length of the 1992 rebuild. v_race_venues is explicit about this: its 'figures' column reads 'as raced' where a layout row covers the year and 'current layout' where it does not. Zandvoort, Suzuka, Imola, Jerez, Estoril, Paul Ricard, Zolder, Brands Hatch, Kyalami and Buenos Aires all changed shape between championship races and are not yet broken out.
known_gaps.resolution: Research the configuration history of each remaining multi-race circuit and add the rows; verify.py already enforces that a circuit's layout rows, once present, form a complete non-overlapping timeline.

known_gaps.description: No fastest lap is recorded because none was set. The race was abandoned after two laps behind the safety car, half points were awarded and no racing lap was completed. This is a true null, not missing data.
